Galactic_Cosmic_Ray_Simulation_Irradiati.description: Galactic Cosmic Rays (GCRs) originate from highly energetic phenomena, likely supernovae or neutron star mergers, within our Milky Way Galaxy. GCRs are composed of atomic nuclei whose electrons have been removed as they travel close to the speed of light, making them highly energetic and potentially damaging to biological material. As astronauts travel outside of Low Earth Orbit they will not be shielded by Earth’s magnetic field and thus, will be exposed to more GCRs, which can be difficult to shield against due to the heavy ion presence. As future missions aim to travel deeper into space, it is crucial to understand the biological impacts of GCRs. Ground-based simulations of GCRs can be used to more readily study the biological effects of this kind of radiation. The GCRSim irradiation at NASA Space Radiation Laboratory (NSRL)/ Brookhaven National Laboratory(BNL) is composed of 33 separate beams composed of 7 different ions (hydrogen, helium, carbon, oxygen, silicon, titanium, and iron), with 14 different energies each of H and He. Specific energies and beam order can be found at https://www.bnl.gov/nsrl/userguide/gcrsim.php

Gamma_Irradiation.description: Gamma rays are a form of electromagnetic radiation (photons), and are the shortest and  most energetic wavelength on the electromagnetic spectrum. This type of radiation is both ionizing and highly penetrating, and exposure to gamma radiation can be very damaging to biological systems. This is especially important in the context of space biology, since astronauts are likely to be exposed to higher levels of gamma radiation during spaceflight missions beyond low Earth orbit. Ground-based facilities allow researchers to conduct irradiation experiments in a variety of model organisms, helping us to better predict how exposure to gamma radiation in deep space might impact biological systems. The most commonly used isotopes in ground gamma irradiation experiments are Cs-137, Co-60, and Co-57.

Heavy_Ion_HZE_Irradiation.description:
Heavy Ion (HZE) radiation refers to high energy ions larger than helium. Despite making up only 1% of the composition of Galactic Cosmic Rays (GCRs), their high charge and energy cause these ions to be one of the most significant contributors to the potential for biological damage imposed by GCRs. Because HZE radiation is so highly ionizing, deeply penetrating, and difficult to effectively shield against, they are a major health concern for astronauts during upcoming long-duration deep space missions. Taken together, it is vital to understand not only how heavy ion/HZE radiation may impact biological systems, but also how to mitigate the damage rather than prevent it altogether. 

GCRs include fully stripped ions to uranium; even-numbered elements, such as carbon, oxygen and iron, are more abundant than odd-numbered elements, although the flux of ions above nickel is low. Some of the most prominent HZE ions in space include Carbon(C), Oxygen(O), Magnesium(Mg), Silicon(Si), and Iron(Fe). Ground-based facilities are equipped with the ability to deliver multiple types of heavy ions at different energies, allowing researchers to study the effects of these ions either in isolation or in combination.

ICE%20FIRST.description: International Caenorhabditis elegans Experiment - First - Aging (ICE-First-Aging) performs an analysis of the aging related protein aggregation and the effects of aging in muscle cells. C. elegans (nematode worms) are relatively simple organisms that are used as a model for a wide variety of biological processes. The ICE-First investigation is a collaborative effort conducted by scientists from several countries which have the opportunity to work as a team to design related experiments that would produce valuable results for scientists across multiple disciplines.

IML-1.description:
The International Microgravity Laboratory I (IML-1)  mission was the first in a series of internationally funded Shuttle flights dedicated to fundamental materials and life sciences research and contained an ARC and a JSC Life Science payload. 

International cooperation during the IML-1 mission enabled participating nations to attain mutually beneficial goals. NASA provided mission management, payload integration, and Shuttle transportation to and from orbit, and hardware for certain NASA experiments. Other space agencies provided hardware that their own scientists and American scientists used. Joint use of facilities in the large international inventory of flight research equipment reduces the cost of space experimentation for each agency. Investigators also shared data and samples so that the scientific return was multiplied.

The IML-1 investigations built on previous knowledge about adaptation to space, adding new information needed to develop measures that enhance the quality of life in space and counteract the potentially harmful physiological responses to microgravity. To examine the adaptation of the human body to a gravity-free environment, the payload crew members conducted experiments on themselves. From these studies, scientists learned more about the reactions of the vestibular, nervous, circulatory, skeletal, muscle, and metabolic systems to weightlessness.  With other animals and plants, investigators defined the effects of microgravity and radiation on growth and behavior patterns, genetic material, bone development, cell differentiation and reproduction and the effectiveness of antibiotics. They monitored radiation levels to identify potential damage to living organisms, and they designed convenient and comfortable laboratory equipment for the crew to use.

The five non-human investigations sponsored by NASA/ARC were the GTHRES, FOTRAN, CELLS, YEAST, and RADIAT experiments. The GTHRES and FOTRAN experiments used the Gravitational Plant Physiology Facility which was designed by NASA to study how plant's growth and development are affected by microgravity. The GTHRES experiment examined how oat plants respond to different levels and duration of gravity, and the FOTRAN experiment examined how wheat plants respond to light in microgravity. The CELLS experiment examined how embryonic bone cells produce cartilage in cell cultures exposed to microgravity. The YEAST experiment examined how the cosmic rays and high energy and charged particles (HZE particles) cause mutation in the common brewer's yeast.  This yeast was selected because both mitotic and meiotic cell divisions could be studied in this organism.  The RADIAT experiment examined how the cosmic rays and HZE particles cause mutation in the soil nematode (roundworm), a well-documented genetic model.

The IML-1 mission was a highly successful mission that added a large amount of scientific knowledge to life and material science research efforts, both space and earth-based.  The mission also created a strong foundation of mutual cooperation between six major international space agencies who went on to work on the IML-2 mission in 1994 and will continue to work towards an international space station and other future endeavors.

hardware.versionDescription:
The Biorack on IML-1 flew with one cooler/freezer; two incubators; a glovebox; stowage; aluminum containers for experiment-specific hardware; and five PTCUs: one at +10 degrees Celsius, three at +5 degrees Celsius, and one at –10 degrees Celsius.

US-2 (IML-1) Configuration:
The experiment also had its own supplementary hardware which was stored in Biorack Type I/O aluminum containers within the Biorack facility.

US 2 Cell Chambers: Each double chamber had two culture wells consisting of a Lexan chamber fitted with a movable piston and a molecular layer of silicone to ease piston travel. The yeast plate had two grooved areas into which Lexan rings fit. Prior to fixation, the piston was pushed down to vent the air inside the chamber. Fixative was injected through the piston with a hypodermic syringe.

US 2 Culture Assemblies: Four of the double chambers (a total of eight culture wells) were placed into a tray and inserted into Type I/O containers. The tray holding the chambers was fitted with a pad to ensure that the chambers were held adequately in place. These containers are opened only inside the Biorack glove box.

US-2 (STS-76, STS-81, STS-84) Configuration:
Biorack on STS-76 contained two incubators and a glovebox, but no active cooling device. One incubator was maintained at 22 °C and the other at 36.5 °C. The incubators each contained new, variable-speed centrifuges, different from those that flew on IML-1. The new centrifuges were equipped with brushless d.c. motors and new control electronics. They could run at any one of three, pre-set, rotational speeds, resulting in three different levels of acceleration force.

On STS-76 the Biorack also contained three PTCUs: two at 5 °C and one at -10 °C.

On STS-81 and STS-84 the Biorack contained two PTCUs at 5 °C.

The experiment also had its own supplementary hardware which was stored in Biorack Type I aluminum containers within the Biorack facility.

Plunger Box: The plunger box is a sterile environment for activating cell growth and fixating cells in microgravity. The box is composed of two culture chambers, each of which holds two 11x22 mm glass cover slips. The chambers are connected to three cylindrical compartments filled with media or fixative. The medium is forced into the culture chamber by manually releasing a spring-loaded plunger. The sealed plunger boxes allow astronauts to activate and inactivate cell growth in space flight and to store the samples for later analysis on Earth.
The ATR-4 was flown on Shuttle missions as described.
The hardware was flown on IML-1 as described.
The hardware was flown on IML-1, STS-76, STS-81, and STS-84 as described.

The Biorack on IML-1 flew with one cooler/freezer; two incubators; a glovebox; stowage; aluminum containers for experiment-specific hardware; and five PTCUs: one at 10 °C, three at 5 °C, and one at -10 °C.

US-3 (IML-1) Configuration:
The experiment also had its own supplementary hardware which was stored in Biorack Type I aluminum containers within the Biorack facility.

US-3 Cell Chambers: Limb bud cell cultures were contained in a Lexan polycarbonate chamber with two wells. Each well had a "bubble" of a gas-changing material, which expanded or collapsed as medium was added or removed. A silicon rubber gasket and bottom plate completed the basic assembly. Cells were cultured on coverslips inserted between the gasket and bottom plate. A deflector ring in the bottom of the chamber prevented fluid forces—produced during the medium injection and withdrawal—from dislodging or shearing the cells on the coverslip.

US-3 Chamber Assemblies: Four culture chambers (eight chamber wells) were inverted and placed on a tray designed to fit into a Type I container, thus allowing the four culture chambers to be removed as a unit. The chamber units were held in place in the tray by double-sided, sticky-backed tape. The medium exchange and fixation were performed by inserting a hypodermic needle through the gasket and onto the cultures on the cover slip.

Syringe Racks: The syringe racks held the syringes used to perform medium exchange and fixation of the cell cultures. The racks, made of Lexan polycarbonate, were designed in three different arrangements such that each one fit into a different location: the middeck locker stowage insert, the cooler, or the freezer. The cooler rack held 40 syringes filled with replacement medium. The stowage rack held the replacement-medium syringes that were transferred from the cooler rack following the Biorack's activation. Finally, the freezer rack stored syringes that contain removed, conditioned medium.

US-3 (STS-76) Configuration:
Biorack on STS-76 contained two incubators and a glovebox, but no active cooling device. One incubator was maintained at 22 °C and the other at 36.5 °C. The incubators each contained new, variable-speed centrifuges, different from those that flew on IML-1. The new centrifuges were equipped with brushless d.c. motors and new control electronics. They could run at any one of three, pre-set, rotational speeds, resulting in three different levels of acceleration force.

The Biorack also contained three PTCUs: two at 5 °C and one at -10 °C.

The experiment also had its own supplementary hardware which was stored in Biorack Type I aluminum containers within the Biorack facility.

US-3 Cell Activation Kit-1 (Cytokines): The kit consists of polycarbonate blocks or "cassettes," each stored in a Type I container. Each cassette is made up of six independent culture chambers and associated daughter chambers. The chambers can be manipulated by turning vanes to connect or to isolate them from each other or by pushing pistons to displace fluid from chamber to chamber. Activators can be added and supernatant filtered from cells by means of a filtering system within the cassette. After filtration, cells can be resuspended into the cassette using a multi-injector unit.

The Biorack on IML-1 flew with one cooler/freezer; two incubators; a glovebox; stowage; aluminum containers for experiment-specific hardware; and five PTCUs: one at +10 degrees Celsius, three at +5 degrees Celsius, and one at –10 degrees Celsius.

US-1 (IML-1 and STS-76) Configuration:
Biorack on STS-76 contained two incubators and a glovebox, but no active cooling device. One incubator was maintained at 22 °C and the other at 36.5 °C. The incubators each contained new, variable-speed centrifuges, different from those that flew on IML-1. The new centrifuges were equipped with brushless d.c. motors and new control electronics. They could run at any one of three, pre-set, rotational speeds, resulting in three different levels of acceleration force.

The Biorack also contained three PTCUs: two at 5 °C and one at -10 °C.

On IML-1 and STS-76, the experiment made use of the following supplementary hardware which was stored in both Type I and Type II aluminum containers within the Biorack facility.

Lexan Tubes: Lexan polycarbonate tubes were assembled in four- and eight-tube configurations in Type I containers to maintain the nematodes in liquid buffered saline. The containers featured CR-39 film to document the tracks made by the radiation, kimfoil sheets to keep the film oxygenated, and thermal luminescence detection packages to measure radiation received.

Radiation Cartridge Belt: The belt, made of Nomex fabric with Pyrell foam-lined pockets and Velcro attachments, as attached to the Spacelab tunnel to absorb radiation. It held five Type I containers and one European Space Agency (ESA) temperature recorder.

Nematode Stack Assembly: Twenty-eight layered assemblies were contained within each Type II container. These assemblies consisted of a base support, worm/agarose layers on millipore filter paper, CR-39 film to track the path of radiation, kimfoil sheets, and Teflon sheets to act as a non-stick surface and to prevent dislodging the worm/agarose layer postflight when removing the CR-39 film.

For reflight on STS-76, major modifications were made to the experiment-specific hardware. For IML-1, the experiment was passive, with no crew activation of the experiment. For STS-76, a crew member initiated the experiment by injecting the nematodes into special lexan tubes. The tubes used to hold the worm cultures until injection into other exposure tubes were similar to those used on IML-1, but one end had a special cap designed for use with a syringe. The exposure tubes for STS-76 were of the same material but shorter and were housed in pairs inside an elemental tin shield. This shielding added weight to each container. A control exposure tube without radioisotopes was placed into an aluminum sleeve next to the tin-shielded tubes. The radiation cartridge belts were also different; for STS-76 they held aluminum canisters with syringes, whereas for IML-1 they held Biorack Type I containers.
The GPPF was flown on IML-1 with all the components as described.

IML-2.description:
An international team of experts worked together to study basic scientific issues unique to space during the Second International Microgravity Laboratory (IML-2) mission.  Through the mission's global approach to space science, the international partners shared the costs of development of equipment and support of investigators, thus reducing the expenses to any one space agency.  Scientists from around the world (13 countries) used the IML-2 equipment to conduct complementary materials science and life science investigations and focus efforts on fundamental questions of interest to the worldwide scientific community. The IML-2 mission objective was to conduct microgravity and life sciences investigations that require this unique low-gravity environment created inside the orbiting space laboratory Spacelab.

The two non-human investigations sponsored by NASA/ARC were the Early Development of a Gravity-Receptor Organ in Microgravity and the Effects is Microgravity on Aurelia Ephyra Behavior and Development.  The Early Development of a Gravity-Receptor Organ in Microgravity experiment examined how the otolith organs (gravity sensors) formed in animals (newts) as they developed from an early stage of development (3-5 days after fertilization) under microgravity conditions.  The Effects is Microgravity on Aurelia Ephyra Behavior and Development experiment was the continuation of an investigation flown on the Spacelab mission SLS-1. The IML-2 investigation examined jellyfish development and behavior in varying levels of gravity.

The IML-1 mission was a highly successful mission that added a large amount of scientific knowledge to life and material science research efforts, both space and earth-based.  The mission also created a strong foundation of mutual cooperation between six major international space agencies who will continue to work towards an international space station and other future endeavors.

hardware.versionDescription:
NASDA Life Science Cell Culture Kit (CCK) - Plant Fixation Chambers (PFCs) Configuration:

The Plant Fixation Chambers (PFCs) were provided by NASDA. They are aluminum, pertri-dish like containers which are approximately 100 mm in diameter by 35 mm high. Each chamber has a 15 mm septum port which extends 22 mm above the top of the container. These containers are completely sealed. The PFCs allow plant cells exposed to space flight to be fixed on orbit by insertion of a chemical fixative via syringe through the septum port. The fixative used was a 3% glutaraldehyde (balance water) solution. 20 ml of fixative was contained within each chamber.

Both the Aquarium and Fish Package were flown on IML-2.

The Aquarium Package (A/P) is a cassette-type aquarium for newts and Medaka fish. It has its own independent life-support system.

The Fish Package (F/P) is a water tank designed for fish. Like the Aquarium Package, the Fish Package has its own independent life-support system.

IRISS.description:
ESA astronaut Andreas Mogensen (DK) is assigned to fly on the Soyuz TMA-18M spacecraft to the International Space Station, scheduled for launch on 2 September 2015.

Mogensen’s mission is called 'iriss'. The winning proposal was submitted by Filippo Magni (a 20-year-old student of aerospace engineering at Politecnico di Milano, Italy) and was selected from over 700 suggestions received from across Europe. The name for Andreas’ 10-day mission combines Iris and ISS. Iris was a Greek goddess, the messenger of the gods of Olympus and the personification of the rainbow. As messenger, she represents the link between humanity and the cosmos, and between the heavens and Earth.

Immune-STL.description: The Immune Space Tissue Loss experiment was the first fundamental biology experiment to conduct an in-flight infection of human cells using pathogenic bacteria. The goal of this experiment was two-fold, 1) to characterize how human cells respond to bacterial infection during spaceflight, and 2) to characterize human cell immune and stress responses to microgravity, thus providing unique insight into conditions faced by astronauts during spaceflight, as well as how cells in our bodies normally behave or transition to disease caused by infection, immune disorders or cancer. The knowledge gained from this work may eventually aid in the development of new treatments for infectious diseases, which remain a leading cause of death worldwide.

SSIP-8, SSIP-10, and SSIP-29 Configuration:

The basic configuration of the AEM included the air filter, lighting, and food subsystems listed earlier. The basic unit was not equipped with a drinking water subsystem. Animals obtained fluids by eating potatoes that were placed in the cage.

Space Shuttle Configuration:

After the Student Shuttle Flight Program, a water box, described earlier, was added to provide a better source of hydration. A major modification was made later to allow in-flight refilling of this water box. This modification added connections on the front panel, appropriate controls, and tubing to transfer the water being added to the water box. New fans were also installed to provide better acoustics and new inlet and outlet filters were provided for better odor control. Cloth mufflers, attached to the outside of the AEM, were also added in order to further reduce the middeck noise level. The inside cage divider was removed. Finally, a holder was made at the rear of the AEM to contain an Ambient Temperature Recorder with holders for two remote ATR temperature sensors. New timers were also installed when it was determined that the originals were no longer available.

Immune.1.description:
STS-60 was the second flight of SPACEHAB, a small, pressurized module developed by SPACEHAB, Inc., to augment the Space Shuttle's working volume.  SPACEHAB provides approximately 1100 cubic feet of internal volume, as well as external surface area. Both internal and external areas can be used for mounting, stowing, and conducting experiments. 

Life sciences experiments aboard SPACEHAB included the Immune Response Studies experiment (Immune.01). Immune.01 was the first collaboration between NASA and Chiron Corporation, the commercial partner for all of the Immune payloads. Immune.01 tested the ability of a proprietary compound, polyethylene glycol interleukin-2, to prevent the short-term suppression of the immune system observed during exposure to microgravity. This rapid suppression of the immune system gives investigators a unique opportunity to study ways to prevent or reduce similar immune system suppression that occurs with some diseases and old age.

LMS.description:
NASA's Marshall Space Flight Center was responsible for the overall LMS mission management and for the microgravity investigations; the life sciences investigations were managed at the Johnson Space Center in Houston, Texas. Four other space agencies joined NASA to support this mission: the Canadian Space Agency (CSA), Italian Space Agency (ASI), French Space Agency (CNES), and European Space Agency (ESA). Each of the space agencies contributed hardware and supported different experiments. 

Thirteen experiments conducted during the Life and Microgravity Spacelab mission were sponsored by US research institutes.  This research included studies in the field of neurovestibular adjustment, pulmonary function, physiology of muscles and bones, energy metabolism during space flight in humans and the effects of space flight on human performance, sleep and biological (circadian) rhythms. The biology investigations included studies on the development of the neural system in fish eggs, alterations in the metabolism of bone in rats and changes in the cell structure of conifer seedlings. 

The research performed during the LMS mission has the potential to significantly enhance the quality of life on Earth. If the structure of certain proteins can be determined with the help of the space-grown crystals, advances can be made to improve the treatment of many human diseases. Space investigations in physiological processes may lead to remedies for loss of bone or muscle mass suffered by astronauts and people on Earth with osteoporosis. Electronic materials research in space may help refine manufacturing processes on Earth, leading to improved products, like computers, lasers and other high-tech devices. Using the unique environment of space to conduct science investigations in biology and physics increases scientists' understanding of these fundamental processes.

MDRV.description: Microbial Drug Resistance and Virulence (MDRV) was a joint space flight research effort of four independent investigators to further the understanding of how the space flight environment affected microbial pathogenic behavior. Three studies examined the virulence of three different bacteria strains, Salmonella typhimurium, Streptococcus pneumoniae, and Pseudomonas aeruginosa.  These studies focused on investigating genetic and phenotypic changes.  Also, MDRV provided the bacteria investigators with a unique opportunity to conduct a collaborative study using bacteria that were exposed to the same space flight conditions on STS-123.  The objective of this collaborative study was to identify common genes and regulatory factors between the bacteria strains that were affected by the space flight environment.  The fourth study investigated how yeast, Saccharomyces cerevisiae, susceptibility to an antifungal agent was affected. Overall, MDRV provided each of the investigators with the opportunity to conduct follow-on experiments of their previous flight microbial studies to 1) obtain independent biological validation of previous flight observations and data, 2) test hypotheses derived from the previous flight data, 3) conduct further in depth analyses on cellular and molecular pathogenicity, and 4) conduct a collaborative study among the four NASA-sponsored investigators that are studying microbial virulence.

MI2.description:
The goal of the Mouse Immunology-2 experiment is to discover how the conditions of spaceflight lead to an increased susceptibility to an infection. These findings can be used to help treat and prevent future astronauts from getting sick, as well as protect people with more vulnerable immune systems here on Earth, such as the elderly or young children.

STS-133 is the 25th flight of the unique Ames Animal Enclosure Module hardware, which was designed to protect animals from the space environment, provide them with plenty of food and water, keep them healthy, and bring them safely back to Earth.

MVP-Cell-02.description: MVP-Cell-02: The MVP Cell-02 mission is a study aimed at understanding how organisms evolve to adapt to the harsh space environment. During the experiment, Bacillus subtilis bacteria will be grown in specially designed environmental hardware and will be housed in the Multi-use Variable-g Platform (MVP) in a range of conditions, allowing researchers to investigate whether the adaptation process occurs differently in microgravity and in the spaceflight environment as a whole. Bacillus subtilis is an ideal model organism for spaceflight studies. It is well studied on the ground and its genome has been completely sequenced. It grows and reproduces rapidly, allowing researchers to grow thousands of generations – and view evolution in action – in just a few weeks. Because bacterial cells are so small, huge numbers of bacteria can be grown in small spaces, allowing researchers to design experiments with many replicates that can pick up even subtle differences between experimental treatments. Information gained from this experiment will help researchers understand the effects of the spaceflight environment on microbial evolutionary processes. This is essential because microbes are both potential hazards and potential tools for human space exploration: while some microbes can be dangerous to human health, others could be central parts of future life-support systems. In either case, we need to understand how microbial evolution in space could influence the relationship between microbes and astronaut crews. In addition, on Earth, the results of this experiment will help advance basic research in microbiology and evolutionary biology.

MVP-Fly-01.description:
Multi-use Variable-g Platform (MVP) is a new commercial testbed for centrifuge-based science aboard the orbiting laboratory. 

What makes the facility so special is its size and capability. Containing two carousels that spin quickly to simulate up to two times the force of gravity, the platform is the largest centrifuge in the U.S. segment of the space station and allows investigators more room for, and control over, their research.

With room for six experiment modules on each carousel, Techshot can fly up to 12 separate modules on MVP at a time. Each module is equipped with temperature sensors, and the box that houses the carousels and modules can be set to the exact environmental specifications requested for any investigation.

But before the real science can begin it must undergo hardware validation. Validation testing of the facility uses Drosophila (fruit flies) to verify environmental controls and check MVP's overall performance. For MVP's hardware validation run, one carousel will stay stationary to allow scientists to collect a baseline of behavior in microgravity. The other carousel will spin at the normal force of gravity on Earth (1 g) as control group. In addition to validating the controls and operability of MVP, this initial investigation – known as MVP-Fly-01 - will provide science data for researchers at NASA's Ames Research Center. MVP is especially exciting for fruit fly research because it can host larger samples for multiple generations. This initial study will look at biological issues common between humans and fruit flies. The investigation concluded in late April, and the modules were removed from MVP and returned to Earth aboard the same Dragon that delivered them to space.

MVP2-Cell-03.description: This project will study the generation of cardiomyocytes, specialized heart muscle cells, for use in research and clinical applications. Specifically, the team is studying the differentiation of these heart cells from induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs), adult cells that have been altered to reinstate characteristics of natural stem cells. Simulated microgravity studies have allowed the team to increase the yield, purity, and survival of cardiomyocytes derived from iPSCs, and true spaceflight conditions are expected to further enhance these effects. Understanding how microgravity improves cardiomyocyte differentiation will enable the team to create clinically relevant heart tissue for use in regenerative medicine, disease modeling, and drug discovery.

hardware.versionDescription: The commercially developed, owned and operated Techshot MVP includes 2 internal carousels that simultaneously can produce up to 2 g of artificial gravity. MVP is used to conduct research in space with a wide variety of sample types, such as fruit flies, flatworms, plants, fish, cells, protein crystals and many others.

Micro-10.description:
Micro-10 is a life science research mission that investigates the effects of spaceflight on the growth, metabolite pathways, gene expression, physiological responses of a microorganism, the fungus Aspergillus nidulans.  The study launched to the International Space Station aboard NASA's eighth cargo resupply flight of the Space Exploration Technologies (SpaceX) Dragon spacecraft on April 8, 2016.

The Micro-10 hardware/payload developer and implementation partner is BioServe Space Technologies, University of Colorado, Boulder.  Micro-10 uses eight Plate Habitats, each loaded with six omniplates that contain cells of the fungus Aspergillus nidulans.  The Micro-10 fungus samples will remain cold until they are activated by warming aboard the space station inside the Space Automated Bioproduct Laboratory (SABL) on May 1, 2016.  Both planned growth periods (4-day and 7-day) for the fungi biospecimens used in the Micro-10 experiment were successfully completed on May 8, and samples returned aboard the SpaceX-8 Dragon that unberthed from the space station and splashed down in the Pacific Ocean on May 11. 

Project manager: Elizabeth Pane, Ames Research Center
Project scientist: Fathi Karouia, Ph.D., Ames Research Center
Project scientist: David J. Smith, Ph.D., Ames Research Center
Principal investigator: Clay C. Wang, Ph.D., USC

hardware.versionDescription:
ISS Configuration:

Currently, there are two CGBA units available to support life science experiments aboard the ISS and additional units available to provide temperature control during transport to and from the station.  CGBA has two configurations: the freezer unit which controls temperature from 16°C to 40°C and the refirgeration unit that controls temeprature from 4°C to 40°C . The internal volume of the freezer unit is somewhat smaller than the internal volume of the refrigeration unit.  All CGBAs offer autonomous operation as well as remote real-time experiment control and real-time data downlink, HD video capability, and high resolution image capture of experiments while inside CGBA.  CGBA is able to run an experiment from cell culture incubation at 37°C to sample fixation and storage at 4°C.

Micro-16.description:
From Space Biology Newsletter - March 2021
The Micro-16 experiment is using the nematode worm C. elegans to test whether decreased expression of muscle protein is associated with decreased strength. The research team developed a new device – called the NemaFlex chip - that will measure muscle strength over multiple generations of worms that will be born and raised on the space station. The animation at right is a short demonstration of how the nematode worms move through the NemaFlex chip where investigators can accurately measure changes in the muscles while in space.

Micro-2A.description:
The Micro-2A experiment will use flight-certified hardware from BioServe Space Technologies, University of Colorado, Boulder. The Commercial Generic Bioprocessing Apparatus is a flight-certified incubator capable of controlling the temperature between 4°C and 37°C and can hold up to 16 Group Activation Packs. Each Group Activation Pack holds eight Fluid Processing Apparatus inserts. The Fluid Processing Apparatus is composed of a glass barrel divided into three chambers that are separated from each another by rubber septa. Each Fluid Processing Apparatus will contain growth medium with membranes in chamber A, a microbial culture suspended in stasis medium in chamber B, and a termination reagent in chamber C.

Launch & Return:  STS-135 / ULF-7 Sortie Flight
Project launched:  July 8, 2011 
Final flight of shuttle Atlantis

Hardware:
*  16 Group Activation Packs will be utilized with one Commercial Generic Bioprocessing Apparatus 
*  Middeck Locker 
*  Eight flight Group Activation Packs and eight ground Group Activation Packs 
*  Eight Fluid Processing Apparatus per Group Activation Pack

Micro-4.description:
Increment 27/28

Micro-4 is a collaboration with BioServe Space Technologies. The study uses special genetically engineered yeast cells to understand how they respond to the physical effects of microgravity to determine the specific strain optimal for spaceflight. Results from this study allow researchers to gain a global perspective on the genes that play a role in survival under microgravity conditions and will allow for a more thorough understanding of the effects of microgravity on living systems.

Micro-6.description:
The Micro-6 investigation examines how spaceflight affects the yeast Candida albicans, a microbe that normally helps us maintain a healthy personal ecosystem in our bodies. However, when our immune systems are stressed, C. albicans can grow out of control. Results from this study will help researchers understand if yeasts are more infectious after exposure to a microgravity environment and, if so, how they have changed.

Critical technology for the experiment is provided by BioServe Space Technologies at the University of Colorado, Boulder. The equipment consists of Group Activation Packs (GAP) stored in a flight-certified incubator at a temperature of 4 degrees centigrade. Each GAP contains eight Fluid Processing Apparatuses (FPA) shaped like test tubes but designed to meet the unique requirement of mixing fluids in microgravity. Each FPA contains an isolated amount of the microbial culture of Candida, plus a growth medium and a termination reagent or fixative. During the three-week flight aboard the space station, a crew member will begin the experiment by increasing the incubator temperature to 30 degrees centigrade, and then activate the FPAs by pushing the plunger to mix the Candida with a growth medium. After 24 or 50 hours depending on the sample, the experiment will be terminated by pushing the plunger deeper into the FPA which combines a fixative agent to effectively stop the growth of the yeast cultures.

Micro-9.description:
Micro-9 is a life science research investigation that examines how spaceflight and microgravity affect the mechanisms of cell biology. The study will use multiple genetic strains of the yeast model organism Saccharomyces cerevisiae to enhance our understanding of how life responds to physical phenomena and physical forces. The study investigates specific mechanisms of yeast cell signaling and response to microgravity. 

The Micro-9 hardware/payload developer and implementation partner is BioServe Space Technologies, University of Colorado, Boulder.  For Micro-9 the hardware includes six Plate Habitats (PHABs), each loaded with seven omniplates that contain cells of the yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae. The Micro-9 yeast samples will remain at 4 Celsius until activation (by warming) occurs inside a Commercial Generic Bioprocessing Apparatus (CGBA) aboard the space station on April 12.
The Micro-9 experiment was successfully terminated on May 9 as the Commercial Generic Bioprocessing Apparatus (CGBA) incubator containing yeast biospecimens aboard the space station was commanded to cool to 4C.  Samples returned aboard the SpaceX-8 Dragon that unberthed from the space station and splashed down in the Pacific Ocean on May 11. 

 

Project manager: Elizabeth Pane
Project scientist: Fathi Karouia, Ph.D.
Principal investigator: Timothy G. Hammond, M.B.B.S.

Mir%2018.description:
Mir 18 was a part of the early Shuttle-Mir science program. Also called the Phase1A program, it was developed as a result of a joint agreement between theUnited States and the Russian Federation initiating a cooperative human space flight program. The program consisted of two long duration missions, Mir 18 and Mir 19, and one Shuttle docking mission, Spacelab-Mir (SL-M, STS-74).

The Mir 18 mission began with the launch of the Soyuz TM21 on March 14, 1995,

Joint research activities were accomplished using both the U.S. Space Shuttle and the Russian Space Station Mir. Twenty-eight investigations, representing seven research areas, were conducted on Mir and/or the Shuttle. The overall objectives of the Shuttle-Mir missions were to obtain engineering and operational experience in conducting research on an orbital space station; to conduct specific investigations in medical support, life sciences, fundamental biology, microgravity sciences, Earth observations and life support technology; and to characterize the environment relative to microgravity and life sciences research on Mir to better understand past and future investigations.

Mir%2019.description:
Mir 19 was a part of the early Shuttle-Mir science program. Also called the Phase 1A program, it was developed as a result of a joint agreement between the United States and the Russian Federation initiating a cooperative human space flight program. The Phase 1A program consisted of two long-duration missions, Mir 18 and Mir 19, and one Shuttle docking mission, Spacelab-Mir (SL-M, STS-74). 

The Mir 19 mission continued the joint science program and began with the launch of the U.S. Space Shuttle Atlantis (STS-71) carrying two Russian cosmonauts, Mission Commander Colonel Anatoly Y. Solovyev and Flight Engineer Nikolai M. Budarin, to the space station.

For the fundamental biology experiments, microgravity was used as a research tool to study the biological development of plants and animals. One investigation studied how weightlessness affected embryo development, returning to Earth a set of pre-fertilized quail eggs incubated to various developmental stages on board Mir.

The Mir 19 mission concluded on September 11, 1995, with the landing of Soyuz TM21 in Russia.

Multiple_Radiation_Types.description:
The deep space radiation environment is a complex mixture of energetic particles and radiation that exists beyond Earth's protective magnetic field and atmosphere. This environment is primarily shaped by two main sources of radiation: galactic cosmic rays (GCRs) and solar energetic particles (SEPs). GCRs are high-energy atomic nuclei, primarily protons (~87%), helium nuclei (~12%), and heavy ions (~1%), while SEPs are high-energy particles, primarily protons, emitted during solar flares (solar particle events) and coronal mass ejections (CMEs).
While it is beneficial and common to study the effects of individual components of these radiation types, it is also important to understand how simultaneous exposure to multiple types of radiation may impact biological processes. 

Studies categorized under this payload would contain irradiation sources from 2 or more of the following radiation types: neutron, proton, X-ray, gamma, heavy ion/HZE, and UV. It would also include any studies with at least one of GCRSim, SimGCRSim, SPESim.

NASA%202.description:
Three shuttle flights supported the Mir 21/NASA 2 mission: STS-74, STS-76 and STS-79. On November 11, 1995, the STS-74 space shuttle Atlantis launched from the Kennedy Space Center to rendezvous with the Mir Space Station.  STS-74 was a nine-day mission that delivered solar arrays to the Mir, as well as a docking assembly to facilitate future Shuttle-Mir dockings. Food, water and other supplies along with Mir 21/NASA 2 science hardware and equipment was transferred to Mir. STS-74 returned to Earth with Russian, ESA and U.S. science samples and hardware. STS-76, launched in March of 1996, was a Mir resupply/return mission similar to STS-74. STS-76 also carried Shannon Lucid, the long-duration NASA Increment 2 astronaut to the space station. She remained on board Mir with the Mir 21 crew, Commander Yuri Onufrienko and Flight Engineer Yuri Usachev, until her return to Earth in August 1996, on STS-79.

Scientific research has always been one of the most important objectives for both the Russian and American space programs. The Mir complex allowed research in fundamental physics, chemistry, human physiology, animal and plant biology, and technology development, as well as investigations directed toward better understanding processes on Earth. A carefully planned program of studies designed to use the known capabilities of Mir was an integral part of the evolutionary process of understanding the effects of long-duration microgravity on biological and physical processes. Scientists had a better opportunity to understand the space environment, study and learn to cope with the effects that it has on spacecrafts and their human inhabitants, and to increase their scientific knowledge, and technology to be implemented on the International Space Station and on Earth.

The commercial initiated research and technology from the advanced technology discipline evaluated new technologies and techniques using the Mir space station as a test bed. An increased understanding of the characteristics of superconductors, protein crystal growth, and the development of biological and chemical systems through fluid processing in reduced gravity can lead to an enhanced technological base for implementation on the International Space Station and commercial processing here on Earth.

Fundamental biology research continued developmental investigations that studied the effects of the space environment on the biological systems of plants. Prolonged exposure to microgravity provides an ideal opportunity to determine the role gravity has on cell regulation and how this affects development and growth. Investigations under this discipline also characterized the internal radiation environment of the Mir space station.

Human life sciences research consisted of investigations that focused on the crewmember's adaptation to weightlessness in terms of skeletal muscle and bone changes, psychological interactions, immune system function, and metabolism. In addition, environmental factors such as water quality, air quality, surface assessment for microbes, and crew microbiology were assessed.  These ambitious investigations will continue the characterization of the integrated human responses to a prolonged presence in space.

The International Space Station risk mitigation discipline consisted of several technology demonstrations associated with human factors and maintenance of crew health and safety aboard the space station. To improve the design and operation of the International Space Station, information was gathered to fully evaluate the Mir interior and exterior environments. This discipline included investigations of radio interference, crew force impacts to structures, particle impact on the station, docked configuration stability, water microbiological monitoring and inventory management.

Space science research collected interstellar and interplanetary space particles to further our understanding of the origin and evolution of planetary systems and life on Earth.

Microgravity research was designed to advance scientific understanding through  research in biotechnology, fluid physics, combustion science, and materials  science. The ambient acceleration and vibration environment of Mir was  characterized to support future research programs.

Earth sciences research in ocean biochemistry, land surface hydrology, meteorology, and atmospheric physics and chemistry was also performed.  Observation and documentation of transient natural and human-induced changes was accomplished with the use of passive microwave radiometers, a visible region spectrometer, a side-looking radar, and hand-held photography.  Earth orbit allowed for documentation of atmospheric conditions, ecological and unpredictable events, and seasonal changes over long time periods.

Nearly all NASA-Mir investigations are joint efforts between the U.S. and Russia, with at least one researcher involved from each country. Sharing of data and results, and the cooperation involved, made the NASA-Mir program a wonderful precedent for future international efforts in space.

NASA%203.description:
The third NASA-Mir mission, NASA 3, began as STS-79 launched on September 16, 1996. On the Shuttle was John Blaha, who replaced the NASA 2 long-duration U.S. crewmember, Shannon Lucid, on board Mir. Dr. Lucid took John Blaha's place on the Shuttle for the return trip to Earth. Blaha remained on board Mir with the Mir 22 crew, Commander Valeri Korzun and Flight Engineer Alexander Kaleri, until his return to Earth in January, 1997, on STS-81.

During the five days of joint operations, astronauts and cosmonauts transferred science samples and data collected by the Mir 21/NASA 2 crew from the Mir to the Shuttle. After returning to Earth, the data was analyzed by researchers.  Crewmembers also transferred hardware and supplies to Mir in support of the health and well being of the Mir 22/NASA 3 crew, as well as to support future investigations on the station. Many of the resupply science items were used directly for scientific investigations performed during the NASA 3 increment.

As scientists learn more about the effects of the space environment, they continue to develop questions from the fields of human life sciences, fundamental biology, biotechnology, materials sciences, and spacecraft  structural dynamics and environment. Valuable scientific information regarding  these subjects was returned from the Shuttle-Mir science program in the disciplines of advanced technology, Earth sciences, fundamental biology, human life sciences, International Space Station risk mitigation, and microgravity sciences.

The NASA/Ames experiments on NASA 3 were Greenhouse.2 and Environmental Radiation Measurements.2.

The commercially initiated research of the advanced technology discipline  evaluated new technologies and techniques using the Mir space station and the Shuttle as unique testing environments. A better understanding of the characteristics of superconductors, protein crystal growth, and the development of biological and chemical systems through fluid processing in reduced gravity will lead to an enhanced technology base for the design and operations of the International Space Station. The knowledge gained also has the potential to significantly improve aspects of commercial processing here on Earth.

Earth sciences research in ocean biochemistry, land surface hydrology, and meteorology was also performed. Observation and documentation of transient natural and human-induced changes were accomplished with the use of hand-held cameras. Earth orbit allows documentation of atmospheric conditions, ecological changes, seasonal changes over long periods and ephemeral events.

Fundamental biology research continued investigations that studied the effects of the space environment on the biological systems of plants. Prolonged exposure to microgravity provided an ideal opportunity to determine the role gravity plays in cell regulation and how low gravity affects development and growth. Investigations under this discipline also characterized the radiation environment inside the Mir station.

Human life sciences investigations focused on the crewmembers' adaptation to weightlessness in terms of skeletal muscle and bone changes, coordination and balance, psychological interactions, immune system function, and metabolism.   In addition, environmental factors were assessed, including air and water quality, and surface and crew microbiology. This set of investigations continued the characterization of the integrated human response to a prolonged presence in space.

The International Space Station risk mitigation experiments consisted of several technology demonstrations associated with human factors and maintenance of crew health and safety aboard the space station. To improve the design and operation of the International Space Station, information to evaluate the Mir interior and exterior environments was gathered. This included investigations of radio interference, particle impact on the station, docked configuration stability, water microbiological monitoring and inventory management.

Microgravity research had the general goal of advancing scientific understanding through research in biotechnology, fluid physics, combustion science and materials science. The ambient acceleration and vibration environment of Mir was characterized to support future research programs.

The variety of science coupled with the ability to conduct investigations over long periods in microgravity, make the Shuttle-Mir missions unique and extremely valuable. Nearly all Shuttle-Mir investigations are joint efforts between the U.S. and Russia, with at least one researcher involved from each country. The knowledge gained will assist researchers in developing future space stations and operational procedures, and will advance the knowledge base of an array of science areas that will benefit all people on Earth.

hardware.versionDescription: The SIGB provided a work area for microgravity investigations that could be physically isolated from the manned environment. In addition, the facility provided a negative pressure in the physically isolated work area with respect to the manned environment using a closed air filtration system (isolated from the manned environment) provided no leaks occurred in the physical isolation system. This air circulation system represented a second level of containment in that nothing could get from the work area into the manned environment without passing through two separate banks of filters. The filters were capable of capturing all solid particulate (>3 microns in diameter) and liquids.

NASA%205.description:
The start of the NASA 5 mission was marked by the launch of STS-84, in May 1997. STS-84 was the sixth docking mission between the U.S. Space Shuttle and Russia's Mir Space Station. Astronaut Michael Foale joined the Mir 23 crew, replacing Jerry Linenger as the fifth U.S. long-duration astronaut on the Mir.  During STS-84's docked phase, water, food and other resupply items, along with Mir 23/NASA 5 research hardware and equipment, was transferred from Atlantis to the Mir. Atlantis returned to Earth with Russian, European Space Agency, and  U.S. science samples and hardware, and Jerry Linenger, who had been on Mir since January 1997. On July 24, 1997, the Mir 24 crew launched to join Foale on Mir and replace the Mir 23 crew. 

On June 25, 1997, during a docking maneuver, the unmanned Progress resupply ship collided with the Mir complex, damaging the Mir module called Spektr. Spektr experienced a depressurization and was sealed off from the rest of the Mir station by the crew. Following this unfortunate incident, onboard activities focused on preserving as much science as possible. The Mir crew conducted repairs to parts of the space station. Some science hardware and research samples were lost, because they were inside the now inaccessible Spektr module. Partial loss of station electrical power also impacted the schedule and performance of life sciences investigations during the mission.

Human Life Sciences research during the NASA 5 mission included studies on the adaptation of crewmembers to weightlessness in terms of skeletal muscle and bone changes, coordination and balance, psychological interactions, immune system function and metabolism. In addition, environmental factors were assessed, including air and water quality, surface microbiology, and crew  microbiology. These investigations continued characterizing the integrated  human response to extended periods of time in space.

Prolonged exposure to microgravity provides an ideal opportunity to determine the role that gravity plays in cell regulation and how this affects the development and growth of organisms. Fundamental Biology research continued investigations to study the effect of the space environment on the biological systems of plants. Specifically, wheat plants continued to be successfully grown in the Svet greenhouse. Research was also conducted on beetles to determine how microgravity affects the insect's biological, or circadian, rhythms. Both the beetles and the greenhouse were maintained during the mission, although a loss of some lighting was experienced. Other investigations in this discipline characterized the radiation environment inside the Mir space station.

Commercially initiated research in the Advanced Technology discipline was aimed at evaluating new technologies and techniques using the Mir space station and the Shuttle as unique testing environments. A better understanding of the characteristics of superconductors, protein crystal growth and the development of biological and chemical systems through fluid processing in reduced gravity will lead to an enhanced technology base for the design and operation of the International Space Station. The knowledge gained also has the potential to significantly improve aspects of commercial processing here on Earth.

One group of experiments specifically prepared NASA for building and operating the International Space Station. These investigations consisted of several technology demonstrations associated with human factors and maintenance of  crew health and safety aboard the station. To improve the design and operation  of the International Space Station, information on the Mir interior and exterior environments was gathered and the station's structure and design was then  evaluated. The investigations studied docked configuration stability, radio frequency interference, the external Mir environment, radiation monitoring and water microbiological monitoring.

Microgravity research has the general goal of advancing scientific understanding through research in biotechnology, fluid physics, combustion science and materials science. Microgravity research included the study of protein crystal growth and characterization of the effect of gravity on alloys. The ambient acceleration and vibration environment of Mir was also characterized to support future research programs.

To better understand our Earth and solar system, research in ocean biochemistry, land surface hydrology, and meteorology was also performed.  Observation and documentation of transient natural and human-induced changes was accomplished with the use of hand-held photography. Earth  observation and photography from Mir allows for documentation of atmospheric conditions, ecological changes and seasonal changes over long time periods, as well as during ephemeral events. In addition, widow surveys were performed to document the condition and degradation of the Mir window surfaces used for  Earth observations.

Nearly all Shuttle-Mir investigations were joint efforts between the U.S. and Russia, with at least one researcher involved from each country. In addition to the benefits of international cooperation, the NASA 5 mission added to the understanding of many scientific areas, including the effects of long-duration space flight on living organisms. Despite the setbacks experienced during the NASA 5 mission, the NASA 5 and subsequent NASA 6 crews and ground-based teams made necessary repairs to the Mir and were well on the way to  re-establishing a challenging science research program to continue the study of life sciences in space.

NIH.C1.description: The life sciences payload on this mission was NIH.C1, a collaborative effort between NASA and the National Institutes of Health (NIH).  The experiments in this payload studied the growth rate, protein production, and differentiation of bone cells in microgravity. Also studied was how muscle cells flown in space mature after return to Earth. To conduct these experiments, bone cells were isolated from chicken and rat calavaria and muscle cells were procured from an established rat cell line. After the Shuttle's 11-day flight, the cartridges were recovered and fixed for analysis. The chicken bone cells showed reduced gene expression for several proteins important to mineralization. Space flight may also have caused a decrease in secretory activity in the rat bone cells. Upon landing, the muscle cells were found to have a fungal contamination, making data analysis impossible.

NIH.C2.description:
The life sciences payloads were NIH.R1 and NIH.C2. NIH.C2, studied the effects of microgravity on mineral, bone, and muscle fibers. Primary cultures of muscle and cartilage cells were isolated from chicken embryos. The muscle cells were cultured as organoids, which contained myofibers and connective tissue fibroblasts. Cartilage cells were cultured in high-density micromass conditions. All cultures were loaded into cartridges and placed into the Space Tissue Loss-A (STL-A) module, which fits inside a Shuttle middeck locker. The automated STL-
A module collected and fixed samples from both cultures during flight. After the flight, the cartridges were recovered and fixed for analysis. Muscle protein synthesis was decreased in flight cultures, but rapidly elevated to ground control levels upon return to Earth. Mean myofiber size in flight cultures was significantly decreased.

NIH.C3.description: The life sciences payloads aboard STS-63 were IMMUNE.02 and NIH.C3. NIH.C3, was a continuation of the studies begun on NIH.C1 to examine the possible effects of spaceflight and microgravity on a number of aspects of osteoblast cell growth and gene expression. In particular, the studies examined the hypothesis that unloading bone cells in spaceflight will result in altered bone matrix production and mineral formation.

NIH.C4.description: The life sciences payload that flew on STS-69 was NIH.C4, the fourth in a series of eight collaborative missions between NASA and the National Institutes of Health. The two experiments in NIH.C4 studied the effects of microgravity on bone cells. One experiment studied whether space flight causes changes in osteoblasts consistent with a reduction in bone formation and an increase in bone resporption. The other experiment observed the effect of space flight on bone-cell formation and loss. Two established bone-cell lines, one rat and one human, were used in the experiments. The cells for each experiment were loaded into cartridges and placed into the Space Tissue Loss-A (STL-A) module, which fits inside a Shuttle middeck locker. The automated STL-A collected and stored cell fractions during flight. After the mission's eleven-day flight ended, the cartridges were recovered and fixed for analysis. In the rat bone cells, no gross differences were found in cell shape between flight and ground samples. A trend was seen toward lower levels of osteonectin and collagen mRNA in the human cultures.

NIH.C5.description: STS-72 included two life sciences payloads—NIH.R3 and NIH.C5—both collaborations between NASA and the National Institutes of Health. NIH.C5, investigated the effects of space flight on musculoskeletal development at the cellular level by means of a computerized tissue culture incubator called the Space Tissue Loss Culture Module. The experiments studied the effects of space flight on muscle and bone cells. Results of this research may lead to development of measures to maintain the strength of muscles and bones during long-duration space voyages and possibly on Earth.

NIH.C6.description: Life sciences payloads on board STS-80 were the National Institutes of Health NIH.R4 and NIH.C6. NIH.C6 (renamed to CCM-A) continued the investigation into how microgravity affects bones at the cellular level. To examine the response of bone-forming cells to weightlessness, human fetal osteoblastic (hFOB) cells were cultured then analyzed for glucose utilization, type I collagen and prostaglandin E2 accumulation, and gene expression for several bone matrix proteins. The results suggest that space flight does not significantly affect these variables.

NIH.R1.description: The life sciences payloads were NIH.R1 and NIH.C2. NIH.R1 included investigators from the U.S., Russia, and France. The payload contained 13 experiments pertaining to the early development of the musculoskeletal, cardiovascular, nervous, immune, and circadian timing systems in microgravity. Preflight, laparotomies were performed on pregnant female rats, both to confirm the pregnancies and to determine the number of implantation sites. Ten rats, each having at least five implantation sites per uterine horn were selected for flight. The rats were flown in two Animal Enclosure Modules (AEMs) located in the middeck. After the flight, the rats underwent unilateral hysterectomies, then were allowed to give birth naturally a few days after the mission ended.

hardware.versionDescription:
SSIP-8, SSIP-10, and SSIP-29 Configuration:

The basic configuration of the AEM included the air filter, lighting, and food subsystems listed earlier. The basic unit was not equipped with a drinking water subsystem. Animals obtained fluids by eating potatoes that were placed in the cage.

Space Shuttle Configuration:

After the Student Shuttle Flight Program, a water box, described earlier, was added to provide a better source of hydration. A major modification was made later to allow in-flight refilling of this water box. This modification added connections on the front panel, appropriate controls, and tubing to transfer the water being added to the water box. New fans were also installed to provide better acoustics and new inlet and outlet filters were provided for better odor control. Cloth mufflers, attached to the outside of the AEM, were also added in order to further reduce the middeck noise level. The inside cage divider was removed. Finally, a holder was made at the rear of the AEM to contain an Ambient Temperature Recorder with holders for two remote ATR temperature sensors. New timers were also installed when it was determined that the originals were no longer available.

NIH.R2.description: The life sciences payload, NIH.R2, continued the NIH's investigations into behavioral changes and the development of muscle, bone, nervous, and circadian timing systems in rats exposed to microgravity in utero. As in the NIH.R1 experiments, pre-flight laparotomies were performed on pregnant female rat flight candidates, both to confirm the pregnancies and to determine the number of implantation sites. Ten rats with at least ten implantation sites per uterine horn were used in the flight group. The rats were flown in two Animal Enclosure Modules (AEMs) located in the Shuttle middeck. Immediately post-flight, four of the dams were euthanized. The remaining dams were allowed to give birth naturally. Pups were marked for identification purposes and euthanized at various ages to allow for examination of the development process.

NIH.R4.description: Life sciences payloads on board STS-80 were the National Institutes of Health NIH.R4 and NIH.C6. NIH.R4 was designed to study the influence of dietary calcium and microgravity on calcium metabolism, blood pressure regulation, and vascular function. Beginning at three weeks of age and continuing throughout the experiment, a group of rats was maintained on either high or low calcium diets. At seven weeks of age, the two diet groups (n=7) were flown on the space shuttle Columbia Animal Enclosure Modules (AEMs) located in the Shuttle middeck. On recovery from the space shuttle and within six hours of landing, the rats' conscious blood pressure was measured; results showed that blood pressure was altered by both diet and microgravity. In particular, blood pressure was significantly higher in animals on low-calcium diets than animals on high-calcium diets, throughout the experiments. This adds to the body of knowledge necessary to maintaining the health of astronauts during space flight.

NS-26-GEM%20(Gene%20Expression%20Microgr.description:
This payload investigates rapid changes in gene expression during the transition to and from microgravity during suborbital spaceflight. The experiment utilizes the brief weightlessness period provided by New Shepard's suborbital trajectory to capture dynamic molecular responses to microgravity exposure.

Scientific Objectives
Document gene expression changes during ascent to microgravity
Characterize molecular responses during the microgravity phase
Analyze gene expression patterns during re-entry and return to Earth gravity
Identify rapid transcriptomic shifts accompanying gravitational transitions
Experimental Approach
The payload contains biological samples (likely plant or cellular material) with molecular analysis capabilities to measure gene expression levels before, during, and after the suborbital flight. The brief microgravity window (~3-4 minutes at apogee) allows researchers to capture transient molecular responses that may not be observable in longer-duration spaceflight.

Neurolab.description:
Mission Overview

Supported by NASA, international space agencies and domestic partners, the Neurolab mission is a dedicated 16 day life sciences mission scheduled for March 1998 which will focus on neuroscience research.  Neurolab's  international partners are CSA (Canadian Space Agency), ESA (European Space Agency), CNES (Canadian Space Agency), DARA (German Space Agency) and NASDA (Japanese Space Agency; domestic partners include several institutes at the National Institutes of Health (NIH) including the Division of Research Grants; the National Institute on Aging; the National Institute on Deafness, and other Communication Disorders; National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute; National Institute on Neurological Disorders and Strokes; and the Office of Naval Research.  Funding and development of equipment and experiment hardware for the Neurolab mission will be shared between all partners.

Neurolab will use the orbiting space laboratory called Spacelab, which can be placed in the cargo bay of the Space Shuttle, to conduct life sciences experiments.  The goals and objectives of the Neurolab mission are:  1) to use the unique environment of space flight to study fundamental neurobiological processes; 2) to increase the understanding of the mechanisms responsible for neurologic and behavioral changes that occur in space flight; 3) to further life sciences goals in support of human space flight; and 4) to apply results from space studies to the health, well-being, and economic benefits of people on Earth.

The Neurolab science payload is organized into eight science teams; each principal investigator is assigned to one of these teams. Johnson Space Center oversees the human life sciences teams:  Autonomic Nervous System, Sensory Motor and Performance, Sleep and Vestibular, while Ames Research Center oversees the four animal life sciences teams:  Aquatic, Adult Neuronal Plasticity, Mammalian Development and Neurobiology.  The philosophy of team development was to merge complimentary scientific objectives to enhance data collection, and to share data collection, procedures, subjects, facilities and/or analysis of results. 

Autonomic Nervous System investigations will study the effects of microgravity on the autonomic nervous system (ANS); specifically, on its role in cardiovascular regulation.  In order to monitor the sympathetic response to various ANS stressors and determine the effect of microgravity on the ANS, measurements of muscle sympathetic nerve activity, lower body negative pressure, plasma volume, blood pressure, cardiac performance by electrocardiogram (ECG) testing, and metabolite levels.

The Sensory and Performance Team will examine the effects of space flight on sensory-motor function, performance and perception.  Several tests are planned to examine the coordination between vision and motor activity during acclimation to microgravity, the compensation for movement in near-weightlessness, and the after-effects upon return to Earth.

The Sleep investigation team will evaluate the normal sleep patterns of crew members before, during and after space flight to identify factors which may be contributing to sleep disturbances in space.  Sleep experiments will examine whether microgravity contributes to the alterations in sleep patterns.  Scientists will also investigate the use of melatonin as a hypnotic agent for the treatment of sleep disturbances and the improvement of mood and cognitive performance of the crewmembers.

The Vestibular System is made up of a cavity situated at the entrance to the bony labyrinth in the inner ear which contains the tiny organs governing equilibrium and balance -- the saccule and utricle.  This team will measure eye movements and perception of astronauts during artificial linear acceleration to determine how spatial orientation of the vestibulo-ocular and optokinetic responses are altered in microgravity.

The Aquatic Team will study the afferent and efferent responses of the vestibular cranial nerve in Toadfish in response to linear stimuli, before, during and after space flight.  The team will also study the development and formation of the gravity-sensing apparatus in fresh water snails and sword tail fish, both of which are planned to undergo significant portions of their embryonic and larval development in flight.

The Adult Neuronal Plasticity Team will examine the neural and physiological changes during and following space flight to address the response in the adult Central Nervous System to altered gravity.  Three critical areas of neural adaptation will be examined:  vestibular and motor plasticity, circadian and sleep/wake physiology and anatomy, and homeostatic regulation.

The Mammalian Development team will investigate the effects of space flight on the development of the mammalian nervous system.  The development of the autonomic nervous system (ANS) and neuromuscular system will be carefully studied and measured so that differences in neurological development in space versus that on Earth can be determined.

The Neurobiology team will research the role that gravity plays in specifying the pathways through which nerves send signals throughout the body.  Scientists plan to examine the sensory neurons which are controlled by genetic and environmental cues in both the development and regeneration of gravity sensing systems in crickets.

The Neurolab mission encompasses many areas of neuroscience research and will allow in-depth study of several species in space.  Currently scheduled for early 1998, Neurolab will continue to undergo further definition and planning in the upcoming years.

hardware.versionDescription: The hardware was flown on Neurolab as described.

Neurolab Configuration:

For Neurolab, the Animal Enclosure Module (AEM) was modified to provide on-orbit access to rodents and to provide a means of transporting rodents from the AEM in the shuttle middeck to the General Purpose Work Station (GPWS) in Spacelab. The modifications also supply a means for changeout of the AEM food bar plates. The hardware provides particulate containment during access and transfer operations. The AEM Access modification consists of six distinct changes/additions to the basic AEM currently in use: 1) Modification of the top of the AEM to provide hatch-type access, 2) Construction of an Access and Transfer Unit (ATU) to allow transfer of rodents from the AEM while maintaining particulate containment, 3) Construction of Rodent Holding Boxes, which hold the rodents while being transferred from the AEM to the GPWS, 4) Food Change-Out Kits, 5) Clean-Up Kits, and 6) Spare Gauntlets.

AEM Hatches: The top of the AEM was modified to accommodate hatches that mate with the Access and Transfer Unit (ATU) in order to permit the removal of rodents from the AEM while maintaining particulate containment for subsequent transfer to Rodent Holding Boxes and then to the GPWS. 

Access and Transfer Unit (ATU): The ATU is primarily made of Lexan, with Tyvek gauntlets and a bladder-cloth sock between the ATU and the General Purpose Transfer Unit (GPTU).  Two hatches on the floor of the ATU seal against the AEM hatches.  The operator uses gauntlets to reach inside the ATU and open the ATU that opens the AEM hatch to access the rodents.  Once the rodents are removed, the ATU hatch along with the AEM hatch is reinstalled, permitting the ATU to be detached from the AEM and allowing transport to the GPWS.  A GPTU attached to the back of the ATU interfaces with the side access window of the GPWS for transfer of the rodents into the GPWS. 

Rodent Holding Boxes: Rodent Holding Boxes are used to hold the rodents within the ATU during transfer operations to the GPWS.  Two Rodent Holding Boxes can be placed within the ATU. Velcro latches secure a lid with ventilation holes on the top to lid to provide air for the rodents.  The Rodent Holding Box is made of Lexan with an aluminum lid.

AEM Food Change-Out Kit: The food change-out kit consists of two foodbar plates with foodbars attached, each stored inside two plastic bags.  For change-out, the inside of the AEM is accessed, existing foodbar plates are removed, and the fresh change-out kit foodbar plates are installed.

Clean-Up Kit: The clean-up kit is used to clean the interior of the ATU and the Rodent Holding Boxes during operations.  It consists of dry and wet wipes and a set of q-tips within a ziploc bag.  

Spare Gauntlets: Spare gauntlets are flown to replace soiled gauntlets after completion of access operations in the AEM.  Each pair of gauntlets, made of Tyvek, is stowed in a separate ziploc bag.

hardware.versionDescription:
Neurolab Configuration:

For Neurolab, several major upgrades and changes were made to the RAHF design. The most comprehensive change was shifting from the outdated controls to a fully-embedded computer control system called the Monitor and Process Control System (MPCS). In conjunction to switching to the MPCS, all of the integrated and removable cables in the RAHF had to be replaced with new cabling that could handle the output of the new system.

Within the Environmental Control System, the Thermoelectric Units (TEUs) were overhauled. The old TEUs had corroded due to moisture and condensation exposure, and as a result had decreased in efficiency. A new water separator system was installed, with improved circulation and less noise output. No changes were made to the Single Pass Auxiliary Fan (SPAF). 

For the water system, a quick disconnect port was added to the front of the cage in the feeder alcove so crew could verify that water is available to the lixits. The drinking water manifolds were overhauled to increase the accuracy of the water counts.

The original built-in activity monitors were removed from all of the rodent cages. For Neurolab, three different rodent cage configurations were created: 1) standard adult cage; 2) neonate/nursing cage; and 3) biotelemetry cage. The neonate cages were modified from the standard adult rodent cage by the removal of the partition between the two standard rodent compartments and the addition of an insert called the neonate rodent filter, which created potential huddling space for the resident dam and her neonates. The biotelemetry cages were wired to transmit output from rodent implants.

Neurolab Configuration:
 For Neurolab, minor modifications to the GPWS were made to accommodate integration of experiment specific hardware for the 9301100 and 9301150 experiments. Modifications included two video cameras mounted inside the GPWS to record activities for these experiments and an interface box mounted on the outside of the GPWS to provide power to the video cameras.

During flight, the Animal Walking Apparatus (AWA) for experiment 9301150 was deployed in the GPWS to conduct the experiment sessions.

Neutron_Irradiation.description: Neutrons in space primarily come from two sources: cosmic rays interacting with gas atoms and dust particles in the interstellar medium, and solar energetic particles during solar particle events. These neutrons have a wide energy spectrum, ranging from thermal energies to several GeV. Neutrons have no charge, and are therefore considered indirectly ionizing, due to their ability to cause instability and induce decay in particles they interact with. The lack of charge also allows them to be deeply penetrating, making neutrons difficult to shield against. Indirect ionization can also have a significant impact on cells due to the high rates of nuclear interaction, and consequently can cause significantly more damage to cells and tissues than other radiation types of the same dose. The ability to use ground-based facilities to investigate how neutron irradiation impacts both spacecraft materials and their biological inhabitants is crucial for mitigating damage caused by space radiation, and for designing effective radiation protection strategies for long-duration space missions.
