OSS-1.description:
Mission Overview

The third Space Shuttle mission, STS-3, was launched on March 22, 1982 and completed on March 30, 1982. On this eight-day flight, the Space Shuttle Columbia carried two crew members and a payload designated OSS-1.

The STS-3 mission was the third in a series of four Shuttle missions that constituted the Orbital Flight Test program. The NASA Office of Space Science, now known as the Office of Space Science and Applications, developed the OSS-1 payload. The primary objective of the Orbital Flight Test program was to assess the performance of the orbiter and its flight systems. Because of this, the objectives of the experiments in the OSS-1 payload were secondary to, and constrained by, the flight test operations.

Nine experiments were included in the payload. Besides observations of the orbiter's environment, studies were conducted in space life sciences, astronomy, and space plasma physics. Specific objectives of the OSS-1 payload were to observe aspects of the orbiter's environment with relevance to plasma physics and astronomical payloads; to conduct scientific observations that demonstrate the Space Shuttle's research capabilities; and to evaluate technology that may be applied to future experiments in space.

The experiments selected used many of the unique capabilities of the Shuttle, such as the ability to carry large instruments into orbit, to operate them in space under crew supervision, and to return them to Earth. In many respects, OSS-1 was instrumental in preparing the way for more sophisticated payloads on later Shuttle missions.

The life sciences experiment was carried on the Shuttle middeck. All other experiments were mounted on a Spacelab pallet in the orbiter's cargo bay.

The OSS-1 plant growth experiment was designed to determine if lignification is a response to gravitational forces or a genetically determined process with little environmental influence. Lignin is a structural polymer that enables plants to maintain a vertical stature despite the pull of gravity. Although lignin is necessary for plant growth in Earth gravity, it consumes a significant amount of a plant's metabolic output, and has no food value. Specific objectives of the experiment were: to test the function of the Plant Growth Unit (PGU) in supporting plant growth in space; to determine the effect of microgravity on lignin synthesis; and to observe the overall development of young seedlings exposed to the conditions of space flight.

Because the PGU was a self-sufficient system, it required little attention during flight. The crew transmitted temperature readings of the growth chambers to the ground several times daily so that these values could be compared to the temperatures of the control experiment.

The Shuttle landing was delayed by one day because of high winds at the White Sands landing site in New Mexico. The experiment teams saw the delay as an opportunity to perform additional science. Unfortunately, science data could not be gathered during the extra day because of the need to conserve the orbiter's energy resources.

Touchdown finally occurred at White Sands after a 194-hour mission. A temporary laboratory had been assembled in a motor home near the landing site. Once the PGU was recovered, gas sampling and analysis, visual observations, and photography were performed. Further analyses were conducted in the investigator's laboratory.

The PGU functioned well in the space environment and was shown to be suitable for use on the upcoming STS-51F mission. Several observations and measurements showed an apparent effect of microgravity on plant growth and development. Plants grew toward the light source as anticipated. Unexpectedly, however, the roots of the plants also grew upward or towards the light source. Positive indications that lignin synthesis is affected by microgravity were examined further on the STS-51F mission.

PARE.01.description: The life sciences payload on this mission was called the Physiological and Anatomical Rodent Experiment-01 (PARE.01). This experiment was designed to study muscle atrophy, glucose transport, and metabolism in microgravity. A ground-based tail-suspension model was also studied during this experiment to determine whether microgravity could be effectively simulated on Earth for the purpose of studying space flight-induced muscle atrophy.

hardware.versionDescription:
SSIP-8, SSIP-10, and SSIP-29 Configuration:

The basic configuration of the AEM included the air filter, lighting, and food subsystems listed earlier. The basic unit was not equipped with a drinking water subsystem. Animals obtained fluids by eating potatoes that were placed in the cage.

Space Shuttle Configuration:

After the Student Shuttle Flight Program, a water box, described earlier, was added to provide a better source of hydration. A major modification was made later to allow in-flight refilling of this water box. This modification added connections on the front panel, appropriate controls, and tubing to transfer the water being added to the water box. New fans were also installed to provide better acoustics and new inlet and outlet filters were provided for better odor control. Cloth mufflers, attached to the outside of the AEM, were also added in order to further reduce the middeck noise level. The inside cage divider was removed. Finally, a holder was made at the rear of the AEM to contain an Ambient Temperature Recorder with holders for two remote ATR temperature sensors. New timers were also installed when it was determined that the originals were no longer available.

PARE.02.description: The life sciences payload on STS-54 was the Physiological and Anatomical Rodent Experiment-02 (PARE.02). The experiments on PARE.02 continued the musculoskeletal studies begun during PARE.01, which flew on STS-48. Together, these two payloads examined the extent to which short-term exposure to microgravity alters the size, strength, and stamina of skeletal muscles normally used to help support the body against the force of gravity.Various assays showed an isoform-specific trend in muscle atrophy, altered gene expression in osteoblasts, altered enzymatic activity in the diaphragm, and changes in some immunological and neurological chemical systems due to space flight.

PARE.03.description: The primary life sciences payloads on STS-56 included the Physiological and Anatomical Rodent Experiment.03 (PARE.03). PESTO.description:
The PESTO experiment will travel in a Biomass Production System (BPS) inside Atlantis' crew compartment during flight. The BPS is an engineering development unit for a future ISS plant habitat capable of supporting long-term plant growth and botanical experimentation in space. The BPS was developed for NASA by Orbital Technologies Corp.

Once the Space Shuttle has docked with the Station, mission specialists will transfer PESTO to the Station's Destiny Lab where it will remain for at least 61 days in orbit. PESTO will study and determine whether wheat plants will produce oxygen during photosynthesis, and purify water through transpiration, at the same rates as on Earth. 

The PESTO investigation, conducted in concert with technology verification for the BPS hardware, measured the canopy photosynthesis (the production of oxygen and carbohydrates from carbon dioxide and water in the environment) of Triticum aestivum (super dwarf wheat). The wheat was grown under high light and controlled carbon dioxide conditions in microgravity. The investigation also measured the metabolic effects on the photosynthetic apparatus to quantify the effects on metabolism and to model the impact of microgravity on biological approaches to atmospheric regeneration.

To test the hypothesis that the carbon exchange rates would be the same in microgravity as on Earth, investigators measured and characterized the carbon dioxide and light response curves for a wheat photosynthetic canopy grown in microgravity. Data came from various sources: gas samples taken from the closed atmosphere inside the chambers; liquid samples taken through ports in the chambers; plant tissue samples extracted by the crew during different points in the growth cycle; and, finally, plant tissue extracted from the live plants returned to Earth inside the BPS. The investigators analyzed the plant tissue postflight for primary photosynthesis parameters, such as electron transport, carbohydrate partitioning, and photosystem (the biochemical pathway for photosynthesis). Measurements were taken over a range of relative humidity conditions to discover whether atmospheric vapor pressure deficits affect gas exchange in microgravity.

hardware.versionDescription: The hardware was flown on STS-110 as described.

PESTO.payloadName: Photosynthesis Experiment and System Testing and Operations

PH-01.description: The PH-01: An Integrated Omics Guided Approach to Lignification and Gravitational Responses: The Final Frontier (Plant Habitat-01) (APH-01) research team's overarching hypothesis on the International Space Station (ISS) investigation is that a comprehensive and integrative multi-omics study of Arabidopsis lines, having different structural lignin contents and photosynthetic efficiencies, will provide new holistic insights at the transcriptome, proteome and metabolome levels. These data will help further establish as to how plants respond to and/or adapt to the microgravity environment; and provide the needed baseline reference points for further exploiting the space environment for plants, whether for fundamental research, long duration missions or human colonization away from earth. Success identifies gene/metabolic networks, mechanisms, and/or pathways differentially modulated at 1 g (Earth gravity) and on exposure to microgravity. This multi-omics study using Arabidopsis, under both 1 g and microgravity conditions (spaceflight), spans phenomics, metabolomics, transcriptomics, and proteomics strategies.

PH-02.description: Plant Habitat-02 examines how radish plants (Raphanus sativus) grow on the space station in different types of light and soils, as part of the ongoing effort to produce food in space. This model plant is nutritious, has a short cultivation time, and is genetically similar to Arabidopsis, a plant frequently studied in microgravity. In addition to helping optimize plant growth in space, this research evaluates the nutrition and taste of the plants.

hardware.versionDescription: Hardware described as flown on the International Space Station

PH-03.description:
Plant Habitat-03 will soon launch to the International Space Station aboard Northrop Grumman’s 18th commercial resupply services mission for NASA. 
Plants exposed to environmental stress, including spaceflight, undergo epigenetic changes, which involve adding extra information to DNA rather than changing it. Plant Habitat-03 (PH-03), led by Anna-Lisa Paul and Robert Ferl at the University of Florida, assesses whether plants grown in space can transfer such adaptations to the next generation and, if so, whether a change continues or stabilizes. The investigation creates a second generation of spaceflight plants using seeds previously produced in orbit and returned to Earth. Results could provide insight into how to grow multiple generations of plants to provide food and other services on future space missions. This investigation also could support development of strategies for adapting crops and other economically important plants to marginal and reclaimed habitats on Earth. Plant Habitat-03 will provide a better understanding of how the epigenome contributes to an organism's ability to adapt to environmental stress, in both current and subsequent generations.

hardware.versionDescription: Hardware described as flown on the International Space Station

PH-04.description: PH-04 launched June 3, 2021, aboard the upgraded version of SpaceX’s cargo Dragon spacecraft as part of the company’s 22nd commercial resupply services mission (CRS-22). The growth chamber, The Advanced Plant Habitat, housed 48 NuMex ‘Española Improved’ peppers. These peppers were grown in arcillite, a calcined clay frequently used on baseball infields for water management and soil conditioning, with  controlled-release fertilizer. The crop underwent two harvests, one on day 100 and then another on day 120. A diverse team of NASA and contracted scientists specializing in space crop production contributed to this work, including an Española, New Mexico, native. The team worked closely with others at multiple NASA centers, the ISS National Lab, and industry partners supporting science on the International Space Station.

PHCF.description: The Pituitary Growth Hormone Cell Function (PHCF) experiment was designed to evaluate the activity of rat pituitary cells in microgravity. Results from previous experiments have shown that rat pituitary cells release less hormone during space flight than on the ground. The PHCF experiment was performed on cultured rat pituitary cells to determine if microgravity affects the cell's capacity to produce biologically or immunologically active growth hormone (GH), and whether any alterations in pituitary hormone secretion remain in vitro after return to Earth. This experiment was also designed to study the effects of microgravity on the GH-producing cell population.

PSE.01.description:
Mission Overview

The Physiological Systems Experiment was launched on October 6, 1990, on STS-41, a four-day Space Shuttle mission. The experiment was designed by Genentech, Inc., in San Francisco, California and sponsored by the Center for Cell Research at Pennsylvania State University, one of NASA's 16 centers for the Commercial Development of Space. The payload was managed by Ames Research Center (ARC). The venture between the three groups resulted in the first commercial space research project in the life sciences.

Results of previous studies have indicated that microgravity accelerates reduction in bone calcium, body mass, and immune cell function. A significant reduction in bioactive growth hormone has also been noted in rats undergoing orbital space flight. The collaborative NASA/Pennsylvania State/Genentech project was aimed at extending these findings through a series of flight and ground-based experiments. Besides its potential commercial value, the project was expected to expand medical knowledge regarding the treatment of human bone diseases, organ regeneration and transplantation, and immune and skeletal muscle cell deficiencies.

Early identification of biologically important compounds would likely provide Genentech with a competitive advantage in the marketplace. At the same time, such knowledge would enhance the U.S. position as a biotechnology leader in the international arena. Private business participation is also particularly advantageous for offsetting some space exploration and research costs.

The objective of the experiment was to test the hypothesis that a growth-hormone-deficient state contributes to bone loss and decreased function of specific tissues in microgravity. The investigators expected that replacement with recombinant growth hormone would retard these changes in the presence of adequate nutrition and exercise.

The flight animals were found to be in excellent condition after the flight. It was concluded that recombinant growth hormone can be preserved for four days, and that osmotic minipumps can successfully deliver the hormone to rats in microgravity. However, an elevated ambient temperature in the Shuttle's middeck may have compromised the experiment's outcome. A series of some 2500 biological measurements and evaluations were conducted by researchers at Genentech and the Center for Cell Research during the postflight period. The results of those investigations cannot be reported here because of their proprietary nature.

SSIP-8, SSIP-10, and SSIP-29 Configuration:

The basic configuration of the AEM included the air filter, lighting, and food subsystems listed earlier. The basic unit was not equipped with a drinking water subsystem. Animals obtained fluids by eating potatoes that were placed in the cage.

Space Shuttle Configuration:

After the Student Shuttle Flight Program, a water box, described earlier, was added to provide a better source of hydration. A major modification was made later to allow in-flight refilling of this water box. This modification added connections on the front panel, appropriate controls, and tubing to transfer the water being added to the water box. New fans were also installed to provide better acoustics and new inlet and outlet filters were provided for better odor control. Cloth mufflers, attached to the outside of the AEM, were also added in order to further reduce the middeck noise level. The inside cage divider was removed. Finally, a holder was made at the rear of the AEM to contain an Ambient Temperature Recorder with holders for two remote ATR temperature sensors. New timers were also installed when it was determined that the originals were no longer available.

ATR data for the two 48-hour delayed ground control Animal Enclosure Modules (AEM) located at Kennedy Space Center (KSC) in the Orbiter Environment Simulator (OES). The datasets represent ATR-4 devices installed in 2 ground AEMs, housed in the Orbiter Environmental Simulator (OES) at KSC/CCAFS/Hangar L/2nd floor.  These AEMs were set up on 6/21/93  (ATR-4 activation approximately 10:55am EDT 6/21/93), installed in the OES at approximately 1700h on 6/21/93, with simulated launch on 6/23/93, simulated landing on 7/3/93, and animals and ATR-4s removed on 7/3/93 (approximately 1200h) , in all cases on a strictly 48-hour delay basis as regards the flight AEMs.

Within each dataset are temperature measurement  timepoints  separated by 225 seconds (3.75 minutes).  At each temperature measurement timepoint, there are 4 temperatures (in degrees C.), representing the internal temperature sensor in the ATR-4 (channel 1), and the 3 external probes attached to each ATR-4.  In each data timepoint entry in the dataset, the data read (from left to right):  time;  channel 1, channel 2, channel 3, channel 4. PSE.04.description: Life sciences payload flown on STS-62 was the Physiological Systems Experiment-04 (PSE.04).  The purpose of this experiment was to study the complex interrelationship between the immune and skeletal systems during exposure to microgravity.  Research has demonstrated that exposure to microgravity rapidly impairs the musculo-skeletal and immune systems simultaneously.  Simultaneous impairment of these two systems also occurs in some diseases on Earth indicating that the physiological controls of the two systems may be linked.

Plant%20Signaling.description:
Ascent on 44P Increment 28; operation Increment 29-30; Descent on Space X-2 (launch/return Increment 34).

The Plant Signaling experiment studied the effects of microgravity on plant growth. During long-term space exploration it will be necessary to provide astronauts with regenerative sources of food. As new information about how plants grown in microgravity emerges, sustainable plant-based life support systems may be developed.

Title:The Effect of Spaceflight on Transgenic Arabidopsis Plants With Compromised Signaling

Principal Investigator: Dr. Imara Perera, North Carolina State University, Raleigh, North Carolina

Overview
Plant Signaling studied the effects of gravity (0 g and 1 g) on the biochemical responses of Arabidopsis thaliana plant seedlings (roots and shoots; wild type and genetically modified plants). Images of seedlings were captured and down-linked to Earth during the spaceflight experiment. Plant samples were harvested at the end of the experiment and preserved for post-flight analysis on Earth.

Approximately 1680 seedlings were grown in space during the experiment.

Proton_Irradiation.description: Proton radiation from space consists of high-energy protons that originate primarily from two sources: solar particle events (SPEs) and galactic cosmic rays (GCRs). SPEs can release a large amount of energy and particles into space, including protons with energies ranging from tens of MeV (mega-electron volts) to several GeV (giga-electron volts). These events are largely very quick and unpredictable, and can pose significant risk to both spacecraft and crew. Protons from GCRs are more consistent but tend to be higher energy, and can accumulate over time to cause more damage to biological systems. Therefore, it is vital to utilize ground-based proton irradiation facilities to understand how this common irradiation type may impact mechanical and biological systems during deep space missions.

ROTIFER-B1.description: The Rotifer-B1 investigation aims to explore the effects that spaceflight has on both the metabolism and genomic/genetic level of the bdelloid rotifer Adineta vaga. This is achieved by culturing rotifers in Kubik, an on-orbit incubator facility. After exposing rotifers to space conditions inside the ISS, samples are frozen and returned to Earth for postflight analyses.

ROTIFER-B2.description: The Rotifer-B2 investigation aims to explore the effects that spaceflight has on deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) repair mechanisms of the bdelloid rotifer Adineta vaga. This is achieved by pre-exposing rotifers to high levels of radiation on Earth and then culturing them in Kubik, an on-orbit incubator facility. After exposing rotifers to space conditions inside the International Space Station (ISS), the samples are frozen and returned to Earth for postflight analyses.

RR-1.description:
NASA's Rodent Research Hardware System provides a research platform aboard the International Space Station (ISS) for long-duration rodent experiments in space. Scientists and engineers at Ames Research Center (ARC) developed the new system for the space station based on the Animal Enclosure Module (AEM) that flew aboard 27 space shuttle missions between 1983 and 2011 and supported studies ranging from four to 18 days. Rodent spaceflight experiments have contributed significantly to our understanding of the effects of microgravity on biological processes that are directly relevant to humans in space. 

The maiden voyage of the system, Rodent Research-1 (RR-1), launched on SpaceX-4 CRS-4 on September 21, 2014, and returned October 25, 2014, during ISS expeditions 41/42. Lasting 37 days, RR1 was the longest duration spaceflight rodent study to date conducted in a NASA facility. RR1 was the first mission to transport rodents aboard an unmanned commercial vehicle. The primary goal is for NASA to validate hardware and demonstrate critical research operations, while supporting the Center for the Advancement of Science in Space (CASIS) in sponsoring the first commercial research study.  Ten mice were flown to the ISS and transferred into habitat.  Five mice were wild type (WT) and identified by an ear notch and the remaining mice, called “Knockouts” had no ear notches. Ten mice were used as ground controls.

PI:  Novartis Pharmaceuticals
The mission objectives of the validation flight:

•	The addition of the rodent research system expands the utilization of ISS for research on the effects of microgravity on rodents.
•	The demonstration of the hardware capability to support rodent research for long-duration missions on ISS is accomplished.
•	A validation of the operational capabilities of the hardware to support rodent research provides valuable information applicable to future long-term space missions.
•	Validate that the Rodent Research Hardware can deliver and maintain healthy animals. 
•	Validate that on-orbit activities to support hardware operations can be performed. 
•	Validate that a limited set of generic on-orbit operations can be performed to support future science objectives including but not limited to euthanasia, gross dissection and sample preservation.

Physiological systems of interest for human exploration of space are targeted at the following systems:

•	Bone loss
•	Muscle loss
•	Immune system changes
•	Cardiovascular system changes
•	Nervous system changes.


IACUC Protocol Numbers:  NASA: NAS-13-002-Y1, CASIS: CAS-13-001-Y1

All animal procedures performed in these experiments were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and use Committees (IACUC) numbers NASA: NAS-13-002-Y1 and CASIS: CAS-13-001-Y1 for flight at the NASA Ames Research Center (ARC) and the Kennedy Space Center (KSC) and the methods were carried out in accordance with relevant guidelines and regulations.

The RR-1 payload produced the following Data :

•	Animal enclosure module temperature and relative humidity flight and ground data,
•	Live Animal Return sensor accelerometer data,
•	ISS cabin and ground simulation chamber environmental monitoring data for ppCO2 and RH (AEM-X (Habitat) telemetry data),
•	Rodent data including preflight data, operations time logs, sample shipment data,
•	Daily Health Check Video
•	Station telemetry data.

Subjects/Biospecimens:
RR-1 Basal controls Dissection performed in Colorado 9/12-16/16. BSP tissues collected from the 10 non-treated control group and shipped to ALSDA.

20 Flight: Flight control group Ab Flight experimental group a-M Ab Mice were scanned by a bone densitometer prior to launch and grip strength obtained. During the mission, near the midpoint of inflight operations, live densitometry scans and grip strengths tests were performed. Mice were euthanized at 42 (+ 3 days), hindlimb dissected and whole blood collected. The remaining carcass was frozen at -80C or colder for return. Dissection performed in Colorado 9/12-16/16. BSP tissues collected from the 10 non-treated control group (Ab) and shipped to ALSDA.

RR-10.description:
Rodent Research-10 (RR-10) investigates the cellular and molecular mechanisms underlying bone regenerative deficits due to disuse on Earth and microgravity in space. This mission examined how aging influences the regenerative potential of the femoral bone marrow stem cell populations.  Specifically, the study examined the role of a gene – Cdkn1a – that produces the CDKN1A protein – that inhibits cell cycle progression in cells. RR-10 (20 female mice, 13-17 weeks old, B6129SF2/J Wild Type (WT) and B6;129S2-Cdkn1atm1Tyj/J (p21-null) to assess the CDKN1a/p21 pathway in regenerative bone formation. The mice will be maintained on the ISS for ~30 days.  This mission was sponsored by NASA.

Tissue degeneration and the failure of tissue to regenerate normally in microgravity are increasing concerns for sustaining life in space, as the duration of future flight missions increase. The cellular mechanisms activated by microgravity unloading in mouse bone during spaceflight are not completely understood, but they include inhibition of the differentiation of bone marrow mesenchymal stem cells and activation of the CDKN1a/p21-mediated cell cycle arrest in proliferative osteoprecursor cells on the bone surface.

In addition to the Flight group, three ground control groups were also part of the study: Basal (representing the pre-launch state), Vivarium (standard vivarium housing for the same duration of time as flight), and Ground (flight habitat in the International Space Station Environment Simulator, ISSES). Twenty mice (10 of each strain) were included in each of these control groups (except Vivarium which included 12 of each strain). These were treated, euthanized and processed on the same schedule and in the same manner as the flight samples. This study includes spatially resolved transcriptional profiling data from hippocampi from 5 WT flight animals, and 5 WT ground control animals. Hippocampi from the right hemisphere were embedded and cryosectioned. Cryosections were placed on gene expression arrays, stained and imaged. Imaging was followed by tissue permeabilization to release mRNA molecules from cells for capture onto the array surface. Subsequently, spatial transcriptomics libraries were prepared and sequenced.

PI: Eduardo Almeida, Ph.D.
Co-Investigators: Elizabeth Blaber, Ph.D., Ruth Globus, Ph.D., Yasaman Shirazi-Fard, Ph.D., Cassandra Juran, Ph.D.

The mission objectives

To test, in vivo, the hypothesis that CDKN1a/p21 is the key effector of cell cycle arrest in bone tissue in response to the stresses of spaceflight, the following specific aims of the Role of CDKN1a/p21 Pathway in Microgravity-Induced Bone Tissue Regenerative Arrest – A Spaceflight Study of Transgenic CDKN1a/p21-Null Mice in Microgravity (Rodent Research-10) investigation are addressed:

•	Determine and compare the extent of osteoblast proliferation, differentiation, and mineral deposition in microgravity and in 1g (Earth gravity equivalent) in a CDKN1a/p21-null mutant versus wild type (WT) mice.
•	Assess whether the coupling and balance of increased osteoclastogenesis and decreased osteoblastogenesis in microgravity is altered in a CDKN1a/p21-null background.
•	Determine whether CDKN1a/p21 expression in microgravity is regulated via mRNA stabilization by the microgravity-induced Cold Induced RNA Binding Protein (CIRBP) in response to oxidative stress in bone.

When completed, these studies will allow researchers to determine whether the presence of CDKN1a/p21 during mechanical unloading in microgravity induces arrest of bone growth and regeneration in vivo. The results from these studies also provide researchers with information to evaluate how CDKN1a/p21-mediated inhibition of osteoblast proliferation and differentiation may be coupled to osteoclastic activity induced by microgravity. Furthermore, these studies seek to connect the potential effector molecular mechanism of regenerative arrest in bone (by CDKN1a/p21) to its inducer, hypothesized here to be stabilization of CDKN1a/p21 message RNA by the oxidative (and other) stress response gene CIRBP.

RR-12.description:
Rodent Research-12 (RR-12), Tetanus Antibody Response by B cells in Space (TARBIS), examines the effects of spaceflight on the function of antibody production and immune memory. Spaceflight is known to have a dramatic influence on immune response, but there is little research on its effect following an actual challenge to the body’s immune system. Using a mouse model makes this possible, as the mouse immune system closely parallels that of humans.  This investigation was sponsored by NASA Space Life and Physical Science-Space Biology.


The mission objectives of the validation flight:

•	The goal of Rodent Research-12, Tetanus Antibody Response by B cells in Space (TARBIS), is to determine the functional level at which spaceflight impacts antibody production. Given that spaceflight disrupts innate population distributions and function ex vivo, it is hypothesized that the spaceflight environment is detrimental to an immune response essential for host resistance during flight.
•	These studies seek to establish a link between exposure to the spaceflight environment, and a reduction in immune system activation. This is significant because this shows how the host’s immunological health can be compromised.
•	There have been very few studies characterizing the impact of the spaceflight environment on antibody responses. Spaceflight studies are inconclusive with respect to the response to an actual in vivo immune challenge.
•	Preliminary studies indicate that the impact on humoral immunity is time-dependent, with decrements occurring mostly after short-duration flights, and enhancements occurring after long-duration flights. Further study is required to confirm this hypothesis.

Specific Aim 1: To determine the impact of the spaceflight environment on primary and secondary antibody responses. C57BL/6J mice are challenged with a TT vaccine either before launch (secondary antibody response in space), or during their stay on the ISS (primary antibody response). Blood and spleen are collected on-orbit from mice euthanized ~two weeks after primary or secondary immunization. Vaccination and assessment schedules are to be matched in ground-based controls.
 
Working Hypothesis: Based on preliminary data, serum and splenic antibody and splenic antigen-specific B cell idiotype levels in response to an in-flight vaccination will be significantly lower than in ground controls. Furthermore, there will be greater decline in the secondary response when the primary exposure is given in-flight, compared to when given preflight. It is hypothesized that these decrements will be due to changes in the distribution and frequency of antigen-specific B cell idiotypes. 
 
Specific Aim 2: Establish that adjuvants that function through Tlr9 receptors are effective during spaceflight.
 
Hypothesis: Spaceflight diminishes many of the cell populations involved in the antibody response (e.g. macrophages, T cells and B cells). Cytosinephosphorothioate-guanine oligodeoxynucleotide (CpG ODN) adjuvants function by stimulating toll-like receptor 9 (Tlr9) to activate and expand these populations. Rodent Research-12 tests the hypothesis that activating Tlr9 signaling reverses the negative impacts of spaceflight on the immune response. 
 
Following sample return, overall levels of IgG, IgA, IgE, and IgM in the plasma is quantified using multiplexed bead arrays, as well as antigen-specific IgG levels via enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA). Stress markers in the blood are assessed (corticosterone and catecholoamines). Antigen-specific B cell idiotypes in the spleen are assessed via RNA sequencing (RNASeq) to determine if changes in the humoral response are due to changes in the frequency, or distribution of B cells that are generated following antigen challenge.


NG-11, previously known as OA-11, is the twelfth flight of the Northrop Grumman robotic resupply spacecraft Cygnus and its eleventh flight to the International Space Station under the Commercial Resupply Services (CRS-1) contract with NASA. NG-11 launched from NASA Wallop's Flight Facility. Research Highlights: The Rodent Research 12 (RR-12) investigation is to study the immune system response of mice to tetanus vaccinations and examine the effects of spaceflight on both the primary and secondary immune responses. When the immune system of an individual animal encounters a particular toxin or pathogen for the first time, it triggers the primary immune response, activating production of early antibodies and memory cells that later "remember" the toxin or pathogen. Subsequent encounters with the same toxin or pathogen trigger the secondary immune response. This consists of a more accelerated response to infection, in which previously activated memory cells quickly respond and produce antibodies that target antigens, the identifying markers on infected cells. Since the NG vehicle does not return to earth RR-12 transporters and samples were returned on SpX-18.

NASA Space Biology Biospecimen Sharing Program Activities

Mice were allocated into four groups: 40 Flight, 80 Ground Control, 80 Vivarium, and 50 Baseline, for a total of 250 animals. Flight animals were dissected/preserved on-orbit by the crew, and the Ground Control, Vivarium, and Baseline animals were dissected/preserved by the PI team at Kennedy Space Center (KSC). Baseline animals were processed on April 19, 2019, two days after launch. The Ground Control animals received the same treatments as the Flight animals on a 3-day delay, whereas the Vivarium groups were processed on a 4-day delay from Flight. All carcasses will be further dissected by the PI and BSP teams during an integrated dissection at LLU. The PI has received the following tissues from all animals: 1. Blood 2. Spleen.  Additionally, the following tissues will be collected by the BSP team, shipped to ARC, and stored in the ISC until tissue recipients are awarded:

RR-14.description:
Rodent Research-14 (RR-14). Microgravity as a Disruptor of the 12-hour Circatidal Clock (Rodent Research-14), uses mice to test whether disruptions to the 12-hour circatidal clock in microgravity affect the body on a cellular and organ level. Previous research established the role of the 12-hour daily clock in maintenance of stress responsive pathways. By exposing cellular systems in mice to the stress of microgravity, this investigation allows examination of cellular adaptation to changes in the daily clock and the effects on behavior.

The mission objectives of the validation flight:

•	The Microgravity as a Disruptor Of The 12-hour Circatidal Clock (Rodent Research-14) investigation documents the effects of microgravity on the biological circadian rhythm at a genetic level by analyzing effects specifically on the liver, but also on other tissues, including the colon, heart, lung, kidney and hypothalamus. Based on preliminary findings, the cell’s autonomous 12-hour clock controls stress levels, protein responses, and coordinates metabolism. The research team hypothesizes that the 12-hour molecular clock is disrupted by exposure to microgravity.
•	The rationale for this investigation comes from recent discoveries that genes associated with the 12-hour clock program are associated with the most common form of liver disease in humans, termed non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD). Although reversible, NAFLD, which is characterized by the aberrant accumulation of lipid in the liver, represents the first step in a spectrum of hepatic disease that contributes to insulin resistance, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and ultimately hepatocellular carcinoma. The essential role of the 12-hour clock for controlling proper metabolic function of the liver has major implications for maintaining whole body energy homeostasis.
•	The gravitational impact on the 12-hour molecular clock and corresponding effects on the metabolic processing, ER stress, and dynamic bioenergetic metabolism is to be evaluated. The collective physiological importance of this newly discovered 12-hour clock mechanism to maintenance of organismal metabolism and health suggests that development of small molecule modulators, capable of synchronizing or resetting the 12-hour clock, would be useful for managing complications associated with microgravity disruption of these clock machinery.
•	The objectives of this study are as follows:
o	To investigate the effect of microgravity on the 12-hour clock from cellular adaptation and its effect(s) on organismal behavior.
o	To investigate the effect of microgravity on the biological rhythms that are defined as self-sustained oscillations cycling with a fixed period.
o	To investigate the effect of microgravity on the epidemiological responses to body temperature, cognitive performance, circulating hormones, and sleep patterns through the transcriptional regulation of this 12-hour program and its relationship to the 24-hour rhythm for maintenance of systems biology.

During the Microgravity as a Disruptor Of The 12-hour Circatidal Clock (Rodent Research-14) investigation, the research team tests the hypothesis that the 12-hour molecular clock is disrupted by exposure to microgravity. Mice are flown and housed on board the International Space Station (ISS) for up to 12 weeks and subjected to a 14-day (minimum) entrainment period of 12-hour light/12-hour dark phase in order to establish a predictable pattern of activity. Video monitoring is used to record the activity levels of each mouse. Upon entrainment, the light schedule is changed to a 24-hour period of constant darkness to establish free running conditions. Immediately following this 24-hour dark entrainment, processing occurs in the Life Sciences Glovebox (LSG), and samples are collected for return to Earth for analysis.
 
Ground control mice are also used,housed in identical hardware, and maintained under matched environmental conditions (temperature, humidity, and CO2 levels). The ground control mice are processed on a 3-day offset from the flight mice to allow for downlink and feedback control of environmental conditions, and to obtain the exact timeline of flight operations so that ground controls can be precisely matched.
 
Rodent Research-14 utilizes existing Rodent Research (RR) hardware, including 4 Transporters (2 for flight, 2 for ground), 8 Habitats (4 flight, 4 ground), and various kits; including those used for rodent food bar change, water refill, anesthetization, cardiac puncture, and blood and tissue collection and preservation. This hardware has been characterized and flown as part of all RR missions on the ISS to date. Transportation and ISS cold stowage assets are utilized for this investigation.

RR-15.description:
The purpose of the Rodent Research 15 (RR-15) investigation is to determine the effects of long-term space flight on osteocyte epigenetic modification osteocyte transcript expression and alternative splicing, osteocyte protein expression and modification, mineral structure and quality, osteocyte morphology and bone vasculature, and on bone loss and histologic/histomorphometric/radiographic changes. Study two time points and will look for changes in DNA, RNA, and protein using an "omics" approach to capture all of the changes induced by spaceflight. Tissue- and cell-level properties will be examined to investigate changes in bone mass, turnover dynamics, and material properties. 

RR-15 (20 male mice, 12-18 weeks old, C57BL/6) to evaluate the changes in osteocyte biology and bone matrix properties that are associated with long-term spaceflight. 10 mice will be maintained on the ISS for ~30 days and the other 10 mice will be maintained on the ISS for ~120-150 days.


The mission objectives of the validation flight:

Bone loss due to the weightlessness of space is a major health concern for astronauts that spend significant amounts of time in space. The development of effective countermeasures to bone loss in space requires a detailed understanding of the biological alterations among cells that control skeletal homeostasis. Those alterations can take on many forms, including chemical modifications to the genome (epigenetics), changes in the expression of certain genes (RNA transcription), and certain small nucleic acid chains that regulate protein production (microRNA), and changes in the physical properties of bone matrix, among others. This study will explore the changes in osteocyte biology and bone matrix properties that are associated with long-term space flight, with the goal of elucidating new mechanisms to target for maintaining bone health during space travel. These experiments will provide insight into the limitations of ground-based models and identify the biological processes for which they exhibit high fidelity to space flight changes. Moreover, new mechanisms fostering bone loss will emerge, which will provide new targets to counteract space travel-induced bone loss.

RR-17.description:
The Rodent Research-17 (RR-17) investigation utilizes mice flown aboard the International Space Station (ISS), and maintained on Earth, to investigate the physiology of aging in response to microgravity and biological age at onset of the progression of disease. The primary hypothesis of Rodent Research-17 is that exposure to the spaceflight environment accelerates or magnifies the effect of changes observed during the aging process, resulting in significant effects similar to the progression of cellular and metabolic dysfunction associated with aging and senescence on Earth. It is further hypothesized that novel molecular targets may be identified by microgravity exposure that can facilitate the development of treatments related to aging. Furthermore, long-duration exposure to microgravity induces a number of gene expression, protein, and metabolic alterations that may be identifiable as a series of assessable biomarkers for the deleterious effects of aging associated with cellular senescence.  This investigation was sponsored by NASA.

In the Rodent Research Reference Mission (RRRM-2), forty female C57BL/6NTac mice were flown on the International Space Station. To assess differences in outcomes due to age, twenty 12 week-old and twenty 29 week-old mice were flown, respectively. To directly assess spaceflight effects, half of the young and old mice (10 old, 10 young) were sacrificed on-orbit after 55-58 days (ISS Terminal, ISS-T), while the other half (10 old, 10 young) were returned live to Earth after 32 days and allowed to recover for 24 days (Live Animal Return, LAR) before sacrifice. ISS-T and LAR mice were the same age at sacrifice. Both the ISS-T and LAR animals had independent ground controls (10 mice per group housed in flight hardware in matched environmental conditions), basal controls (10 mice per group sacrificed 2 days before launch), and vivarium controls (10 mice per group housed within standard vivarium habitats). Thus RRRM-2 included a total of 160 mice. This study includes single nuclei transcriptomics and epigenomics from left cerebral hemispheres from 4 young ISS-T spaceflight animals, 5 old ISS-T spaceflight animals, 5 young ISS-T ground control animals, and 4 young ISS-T ground control animals.

RR-18.description:
The purpose of this Rodent Research investigation is to characterize the impact of spaceflight on mouse retinal vasculature and tissue remodeling and study the role of mitochondria in regulating oxidative stress-induced cellular damage and cell-cell interactions in the function of the blood-retina-barrier (BRB). Also, determine the extent to which an antioxidant metalloporphyrin protects against spaceflight environment-induced changes in retinal neurovascular coupling and retinal function. 

The Rodent Research-18 (RR-18) flight experiment launched on SpX24 on December 21, 2021, at 5:06 am Eastern Standard Time (EST) from Kennedy Space Center (KSC). Forty male mice were flown in two Rodent Transporters and were transferred to four Rodent Habitats upon arrival to the International Space Station (ISS). The mice will receive weekly antioxidant or saline treatments during their stay abroad the ISS. Twenty-six mice returned to Earth live in late January 2022. Some of them will be subjected to a 6-month readaptation experiment at the PI's lab in Loma Linda University (LLU). Fourteen mice will remain on the ISS for ~85 days and will be euthanized and processed on-orbit with sample return on SpaceX-25. Ground Control (GC) and Vivarium Control (VC) groups are maintained at Roskamp Institute (Sarasota, FL) and will follow the flight timeline with a 5-day and 8-day delay, respectively


Principal Investigator: Xiao (Vivien) Wen Mao, Ph.D.
Co-Investigators: Michael Pecaut, Ph.D., Shu-Wei (Richard) Sun, Ph.D., James Crapo, Ph.D. Science Sponsor: Space Biology 


The mission objectives of the validation flight:

Aim 1: Define the relationships between spaceflight condition-induced oxidative stress in ROS expression and retinal vascular remodeling and BRB function in mature female mice during flight and after return to Earth alive. Cellular oxidative status is correlated with changes in retinal vascular topology, vascular endothelial cells, astrocytes, photoreceptors, BRB integrity, and vision function using neuropathology, stereological and automated image analyses, non-invasive MRI diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) and visual electroretinography (ERG).
 
Aim 2: Determine whether spaceflight condition-induced oxidative damage in the retina is mediated through photoreceptor mitochondrial ROS production. The following are to be analyzed using Western blot assays and histopathology: mitochondrial ROS production, mitochondrial associated-apoptosis and mitochondrial integrity in retinal photoreceptor.
 
Aim 3: Determine the extent to which the antioxidant metalloporphyrin protects against spaceflight environment-induced changes in retinal neurovascular coupling and retinal function. Mice are treated weekly with the antioxidant MnTnBuOE-2-PyP5+ (BuOE) a week before launch and during spaceflight exposure. The neurovascular interaction is examined to determine the degree to which neurovascular unit (NVU) and BRB function is corrected and/or reestablished in metalloporphyrin-treated mice when compared to non-treated flight or ground controls.

RR-19.description:
The Rodent Research 19 (RR19) investigation entitled "Mighty Mice in Space: Pre-clinical Evaluation of a Broad Spectrum Myostatin Inhibitor to Prevent Muscle and Bone Loss Due to Disuse project" explores the efficacy of inhibiting myostatin/activin signaling in mice in a microgravity environment in order to preserve their muscle and/or bone mass, or to enhance the recovery of their skeletal muscle and bone mass after their return to Earth. It is hoped that the results of this research will yield novel treatment options for muscle and bone loss in humans, in the contexts of spaceflight as well as various pathologies on Earth.

RR19 will launch 40 female mice (C57BL/6J, 8 MSTN -/- knock-out, 32 wild type, aged 10-12 weeks) on SpaceX CRS-19, and begin ground control studies with the same number and type of research subjects on a three-day delay. RR-20.description:
Current evidence from three space shuttle missions (STS-131, STS-133, and STS-135) demonstrated that ovarian function is severely disrupted in female mice, rendering these adult female mice likely infertile. Both ovarian folliculogenesis and luteal function were disrupted as was uterine function likely as a result of the unbalanced ovarian steroid support. Previous observations raised important fundamental questions on maintenance of female reproductive health that need to be addressed prior to conducting complex multigenerational studies in mammals under space flight conditions. Previous biospecimens collection like RR-1, can add greatly to our current knowledge base by addressing several important intermediate questions that were not addressable in the STS flights. These include an increase in exposure to space flight and collection of adult tissue prior to reentry. So, these studies, will provide for the first time the ability to examine adult ovarian/uterine tissues following long term exposure to space flight without the confounding effects of stress of the reentry.  This mission was sponsored by NASA's Space Biology Program in partnership with NASA's Science Mission Directorate.

These samples will be examined using standard molecular techniques, including quantitative RT-PCR, western blot as well as radioimmunoassay (RIA) for estrogen and progesterone. The team will use steroid (estrogen/progesterone) content of the ovary as determined by RIA as a surrogate for establishing the functional ovarian status of the RR-1 females at the time of their sacrifice. Additionally, key regulatory genes known to be markers of ovarian functional status, including those involved in estrogen and progesterone synthesis (i.e., aromatase, steroidogenic acute regulatory protein, P450 side chain cleave and steroid receptors, etc.) will be examined in ovarian and uterine tissues.

This study consists of 5 experimental groups: 
•	Flight (FLT), n -40 mice (20 mice dissected on-orbit, 20 Live Animal Return (LAR) 
mice),
•	Habitat Ground Control (HGC), n-40 mice,
•	Vivarium Ground Control (VGC), n-40 mice,
•	Vivarium Ground Control Plus (VGC+), n-20 mice,
•	Baseline Ground Control (BGC), n-20 mice.

Principal Investigator: Lane K. Christenson, Ph.D., University of Kansas Medical Center Co-Investigators: Joshua Alwood, Ph.D., NASA Ames Research Center, April Ronca, Ph. D., NASA Ames Research Center, Stephanie Puukila, Ph. D., NASA Ames Research Center
Science Sponsor: Space Biology 


The mission objectives of the validation flight:

 Aim 1. Determine the source (microgravity or re-entry) of the spaceflight-disrupted ovarian function previously observed on short-duration missions. The working hypothesis is that disrupted ovarian function is due to a failure of the periovulatory follicle to ovulate and form a functional corpus luteum. To test this hypothesis, the mice are to undergo a timed follicular stimulation protocol followed by evaluation of established temporally expressed ovarian markers, ovulation, and luteal development immediately following return from space and are compared to mice maintained on the International Space Station and processed identically. This study seeks, for the first time, to determine whether space-induced loss of ovarian function is due to an intrinsic ovarian defect or is a problem with hypothalamic/pituitary support.
 
Aim 2. Determine the fertility (i.e., the ability of ovulate a mature oocyte) in adult female mice following extended (48-60 days) exposure to microgravity. Currently, it is unknown whether females are fertile in space. To address this question, the mice undergo a follicular stimulation and ovulatory protocol in flight, and fertility and tissue biomarkers are evaluated.
 
Aim 3. Determine whether adult female mice exposed to spaceflight are fertile upon return to Earth. The working hypothesis for this aim is that upon return to Earth, fertility will return. To test this hypothesis, flight mice are exposed to male mice after an initial recovery period, and mating reproductive behavior, estrous cyclicity, early embryo implantation, and health and development of F1 offspring are evaluated. These studies provide the first ever examination of long-term space exposure on the female reproductive behavior/physiology, and germ-line stability.
 
In all three specific aims, collection of adrenal tissues allows the research team to determine whether spaceflight-induced stress is occurring. Uterine and bone (femur) tissues are used to address the secondary hypothesis observing the long-term spaceflight effects on ovarian estrogen-responsive tissues. Ultimately, findings of the proposed studies provide critical foundational data to aid in better understanding the impact spaceflight has on female astronaut health.

RR-23.description:
Effects of Microgravity on Ocular Vascular Hydrodynamics, or Rodent Research-23 (RR-23), studies function of arteries, veins, and lymphatic structures in the eye and changes in the retina before and after spaceflight. The aim is to clarify whether these vascular changes impair visual function. At least 40 percent of astronauts experience vision impairment known as Spaceflight-Associated Neuro-ocular Syndrome (SANS) on long-duration spaceflights, which could adversely affect mission success.  Some astronauts who complete long-duration spaceflights experience Spaceflight-Associated Neuro-Ocular Syndrome, or SANS, a condition in which the eyes show physical changes, such as swelling, folding or flattening of different structures of the eye that can lead to decreased quality of near vision. These changes have the potential to affect the success of spaceflights to destinations like the Mars, which will be considerably longer missions than those attempted so far. The information gathered from RR-23 will inform scientists who are working to create effective countermeasures that will protect future astronauts from developing SANS.  This investigation was sponsored by NASA.

Rodent Research-23 will study the effects of spaceflight on the eyes, specifically on the structure and function of the arteries, veins, and lymphatic vessels that are needed to maintain vision. Mice will be housed aboard the station for five weeks and then returned to Earth where researchers will examine the eyes of the mice for changes caused by the time spent in space.

RR-23 flight subjects: Twenty (20) mice (male, C57BL/6J, 16-17 weeks old) were launched in one Transporter on SpaceX-21 (SpX-21) on December 6, 2020. The Flight mice were transferred into two Rodent Habitats upon arrival to the International Space Station (ISS) and were maintained in microgravity for 38 days. The Flight mice were transferred into a Transporter and returned to Earth for Live Animal Return (LAR) on SpX-21 (January 13th, 2021). After Atlantic Ocean splashdown, the LAR Flight mice were transported via helicopter to Kennedy Space Center. There was no testing or procedures done to the animals while aboard the ISS.

PI: David Zawieja, Ph.D.
Co-Investigators: Pooneh Bagher, Ph.D., Anatoliy Gashev, Ph.D., Travis Hein, Ph.D., Binu Tharakan, Ph.D., Stuart M. C. Lee, Ph.D., Brandon R. Macias, Ph.D., and Linda Loerch 


The mission objectives of the validation flight:

These findings, combined with several related studies, will create a more comprehensive understanding of the impacts of weightlessness on SANS during human spaceflight. New insights into SANS from this research are anticipated to shed light on vascular complications connected to eye diseases found in humans on Earth, such as diabetic macular edema which is a common problem for diabetics who have damage in the blood vessels due to increased pressure in the eye, and ocular hypertension, or high pressure in the eye. In this way, these findings will allow researchers to develop more advanced preventative care strategies and treatments for patients here on Earth.

A subset of each group of mice undergoes post-flight testing including Intraocular Pressure (IOP), ultrasound, and Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT) measurements. Post-flight operations include collecting ocular hydrodynamic data (IOP, OCT, and ultrasound), measuring retinal microvascular permeability, blood from the heart, and dissecting the heart, both eyes with optic nerve, ophthalmic vessels, carotid arteries, heart, mesentery/GI tissue (cecum, colon, duodenum, jejunum, ileum), brain, cervical/ophthalmic lymph nodes with surrounding tissues, and popliteal lymph nodes.

RR-2C.description:
Rodent Research 2 (RR-2) launched on April 14, 2015 as the second life science research mission utilizing the Rodent Research Hardware System designed by NASA Ames Research Center as a research platform for the International Space Station (ISS). The Center for the Advancement of Science in Space (CASIS) sponsored Novartis lead scientist Samuel Cadena for the commercial research study. CASIS also partnered with the Department of Defense Space Test Program to assess biomarker changes in a variety of tissues following long-duration exposure to spaceflight. The research performed through the RR2 experiment aimed to illustrate the potential use of mice in space to model human cardiovascular, immunological, ocular, metabolic and neurological diseases and disorders. The findings could lead to new treatments in osteoporosis and muscle wasting. 

The RR-2 payload included twenty female experiment mice (strain: C57BL/6J) that were fourteen to eighteen weeks old at the time of launch. Twenty mice were housed in one Transporter (SN 008) for ascent and on April 19, 2015, five days in the transporter, they were transferred into two habitats (ten mice each, five on each side) for long-term habitation onboard the ISS. Two Animal Access Units (AAU, SN 001 and SN 003) were made available for onboard transfers. The mice were processed over four dissection sessions at one, two, four, and eight weeks of microgravity exposure. Divided into four groups of five, each group was processed identically. Ground controls included the vivarium habitat. In order to evaluate structural and molecular changes over time, mice were exposed to the spacecraft environment for various durations: Group 1 for six to eight days, Group 2 for thirteen to fifteen days, Group 3 for twenty-six to thirty days, and group 4 for fifty-four to fifty-eight days.  

The mission objectives

The primary objective of this research is to monitor the effects of the space environment on the musculoskeletal and neurological systems of mice as model organisms of human health and disease. This project will help ISS U.S. National Lab investigators to discover new molecular targets that can facilitate the development of novel therapeutics for the treatment of muscle and bone-related diseases.  Specifically, time-dependency of morphological and molecular changes in the musculoskeletal system of mice exposed to the spaceflight environment (CASIS RR2) were investigated.

Physiological systems of interest for human exploration of space are targeted at the following systems:
•	Bone loss
•	Muscle loss
•	Immune system changes
•	Cardiovascular system changes
•	Nervous system changes.

RR-3.description:
The Rodent Research-3 (RR-3) mission was sponsored by the pharmaceutical company Eli Lilly and Co. and the Center for the Advancement of Science in Space to study the effectiveness of a potential countermeasure for the loss of muscle and bone mass that occurs during spaceflight. Twenty BALB/c, 12-weeks old female mice (ten controls and ten treated) were flown to the ISS and housed in the Rodent Habitat for 39-42 days. Twenty mice of similar age, sex and strain were used for ground controls housed in identical hardware and matching ISS environmental conditions. Basal controls were housed in standard vivarium cages. Spaceflight, ground controls and basal groups had blood collected, then were euthanized, had one hind limb removed, and finally whole carcasses were stored at -80 C until dissection. All mice in this data set received only the control/sham injection. Microdissection of retinae from previously frozen eyes and RNA isolation were performed in the laboratory of Dr. Xiao Mao at Loma Linda University.

The goal was to evaluate a potential new treatment for skeletal muscle wasting and weakness. Working with NASA, the researchers assessed its ability to prevent these conditions in mice exposed to long-duration spaceflight. Rodent research models have made it possible to study serious diseases involving muscle atrophy, and even age-related weakness. Conducting this study during spaceflight provided the researchers with the rare opportunity to expose all the muscles of an organism to conditions that will produce atrophy – something not easily achieved on Earth.

The mission objectives

Although the primary research focus of Rodent Research-3 is skeletal muscle, the investigators were studying other organ systems, such as bone, both at the tissue and molecular levels. Their goal is to characterize tissue responses to spaceflight and observe how these changes vary with the length of time spent in microgravity. The findings will advance our understanding of the risks that long-term space exploration poses to astronauts and can be applied towards the development of countermeasures to protect astronaut health.

RR-4.description:
Rodent Research on the International Space Station (ISS) continues with the fourth mission launching aboard SpaceX-10. The science on Rodent Research-4 is sponsored by the Department of Defense (DoD) Space Test Program and the Center for Advancement of Science in Space (CASIS), manager of the ISS National Laboratory. 

The primary objectives are to better understand bone healing and bone tissue regeneration and to study the impacts of microgravity on these processes. Experiment results may help to evaluate the practicality of growing complex bone tissues in spaceflight as well as study the effects of microgravity on bone density. RR-4 launched 40 mice (~9-12 weeks old, male, C57BL/6) on SpX10 to characterize the biological and molecular events associated with tissue regeneration.

Although reduced gravity induces cell proliferation and propagation, which is favorable for tissue regeneration, immunological responses are delayed in this environment. Therefore, microgravity presents a contrasting environment for the healing process. The results from this experiment may help scientists evaluate the practicality of growing complex bone tissues in spaceflight and examine molecular mechanisms underlying the negative effects of microgravity on bone density.

The mission objectives

1. To characterize the biological events associated with the healing and tissue regeneration process in spaceflight.
2. To gauge the therapeutic success of certain osteoinductive agents capable of inducing bone healing and regeneration in spaceflight.
3. To evaluate the transcriptomic, epigenomic, proteomic, metabolomic, and metagenomic (microbiome) aspects of the selected biomaterials critical for bone healing and regeneration, as well as sort and integrate the pan-omics results to discover regeneration mechanisms.
4. To use these methods to identify novel biomarkers of bone regeneration, loss, and healing.

RR-5.description:
RR-5 launched 40 mice (~32 weeks old, female, BALB/c) on SpX11 to determine if treatment with NELL1 can reduce or prevent bone loss. 20 mice were maintained for ~30 days in microgravity and then returned live (Live Animal Return-LAR) for dissection at the PI institution and the other 20 mice were maintained in microgravity for ~9 weeks and dissected on-orbit. Samples from the Systemic Therapy of NELL-1 for osteoporosis returned as part of an investigation using rodents as models to test a new drug that can both rebuild bone and block further bone loss, improving crew health. When people and animals spend extended periods of time in space, they experience bone density loss, or osteoporosis. In-flight countermeasures, such as exercise, prevent it from getting worse, but there isn't a therapy on Earth or in space that can restore bone density. The results from this ISS National Laboratory-sponsored investigation are built on previous research also supported by the National Institutes for Health and could lead to new drugs for treating bone density loss in millions of people on Earth.

The mission objectives

The objective of the Rodent Research-5 (RR-5) study was to evaluate bone loss in mice under microgravity conditions and to determine if treatment with NELL1 can reduce or prevent bone loss that would otherwise occur in microgravity. RR-5 launched 40 mice (~32 weeks old, female, BALB/c) on SpX11 to determine if treatment with NELL1 can reduce or prevent bone loss. 20 mice were maintained for ~30 days in microgravity and then returned live (Live Animal Return-LAR) for dissection at the PI institution and the other 20 mice were maintained in microgravity for ~9 weeks and dissected on-orbit. 

All animal procedures performed in these experiments were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committees (IACUC) number NAS-16-001-Y1 for flight at the NASA Ames Research Center (ARC) and the Kennedy Space Center (KSC) and the methods were carried out in accordance with relevant guidelines and regulations.

The Center for the Advancement of Science in Space (CASIS) has formed a partnership with the University of California at Los Angeles (UCLA) to evaluate bone atrophy under microgravity conditions and to evaluate a novel therapeutic to mitigate bone loss. Samples from the Systemic Therapy of NELL-1 for osteoporosis returned as part of an investigation using rodents as models to test a new drug that can both rebuild bone and block further bone loss, improving crew health. When people and animals spend extended periods of time in space, they experience bone density loss, or osteoporosis. In-flight countermeasures, such as exercise, prevent it from getting worse, but there isn't a therapy on Earth or in space that can restore bone density. The results from this ISS National Laboratory-sponsored investigation are built on previous research also supported by the National Institutes for Health and could lead to new drugs for treating bone density loss in millions of people on Earth.

NASA Space Biology Biospecimen Sharing Program Activities 
The NASA Space Biology Biospecimen Sharing Program collected biospecimens from RR-5 to maximize the scientific return from the biological spaceflight. Forty mice (female; BALB/c; 32 weeks old; Taconic), launched in two Transporters (20 mice per), then were transferred to Rodent Habitats onboard the International Space Station (ISS) and maintained in microgravity for ~30 days until Live Animal Return (N-20; LAR to UCLA) or for ~9 weeks total which were ISS Terminal (N-20; IT). There was a Baseline of subjects at KSC. A Ground Control group mimicked LAR, which was housed at KSC, then shipped live to UCLA. There was a Ground Control group at KSC which mimicked flight. All animals were kept on a temperature controlled (~28˚C), 12-hr Light/Dark Cycle.

The unused Diaphragm and tail tissues were set to the NASA Biological Institutional Scientific Collection and made available for request.

RR-6.description:
The Rodent Research-6 (RR-6) mission uses mice flown aboard the International Space Station (ISS) and maintained on Earth to test drug delivery systems for combatting muscular breakdown in space or during disuse conditions. RR-6 includes several groups of mice selectively treated with a placebo or implanted with a nanochannel drug delivery chip that administers compounds meant to maintain muscle in low gravity/disuse conditions. Two groups of 20 mice will be flown aboard the ISS for durations of one and two months. The first group of treated and control mice returns to Earth live after approximately 30 days. The second group of animals remains on the ISS for approximately 60 days. In both cases, animals are euthanized humanely, and tissue samples are harvested for subsequent study and comparison with Earth-based control groups. 40 mice (~35 weeks old, female, C57BL/6) on SpX13. 20 mice were maintained for ~30 days in microgravity and then returned live to Earth.  This mission was sponsored for the ISS National Lab.

The mission objectives

The objective of the Rodent Research-6 (RR-6) study was to evaluate muscle atrophy in mice during spaceflight and to test the efficacy of a novel therapeutic to mitigate muscle wasting. The experiment involved an implantable subcutaneous nanochannel delivery system (nDS; between scapula), which delivered the drug formoterol (FMT; a selective Beta-2 adrenoceptor agonist), over the course of time. To this end, a cohort of forty 32-weeks-old female C57BL/6NTac mice were either sham operated or implanted with vehicle or treatment-filled nDS and launched in two Transporters (20 mice per Transporter) on SpaceX-13 on December 15, 2017. They were transferred to Rodent Habitats onboard the International Space Station (ISS) and maintained in microgravity for 29 days (N-20, Live Animal Return [LAR]), or greater than 50 days (N-20, ISS Terminal).

RR-7.description:
The Rodent Research (RR-7) investigation examines how the space environment affects the community of microorganisms in the gastrointestinal tract of mice (also known as the microbiota). It also looks at microgravity’s effects on multiple physiological systems known to be affected by the microbiota, including the gastrointestinal, immune, metabolic, circadian, and sleep systems. These studies should help explain mechanisms underlying interactions between these systems and the role of the microbiota in these interactions.  This mission was sponsored for the ISS National Lab.

Identifying these mechanisms will provide new avenues for possible countermeasures to ensure the safety and health of astronauts on long-duration spaceflight missions. RR-7 launched on SpX15 (20 female mice, ~10-12 weeks old, C57BL/6J and C3H/HeJ in two Rodent Habitats.) to evaluate how the space environment affects intestinal microbiota.  10 mice were maintained on the ISS for ~30 days and the remaining 10 mice were maintained on the ISS for up to 90 days.

PIs:  Fred Turek
Co-Investigators: Stefan Green, Ali Keshavarzian, Christopher Forsyth, and Martha Vitaterna 


The mission objectives

Samples of food swabs from living surfaces and fecal pellets were collected from each animal before launch and regularly during the mission. The mission also involved extended video collection (48 hr video segments per Habitat) to monitor circadian rhythms and on-orbit mass measurement.

For this flight, 20 female mice of two different strains are flown to meet the science objectives. Animals are transferred from the Transporter into two Habitats that provide long duration housing abroad the ISS. Fecal pellets from each animal are collected before launch, and at each food bar change out (every 14 days). Samples swabbed from the food bar surfaces are also collected for analysis. Swabs of the Habitats are performed preflight, in flight, and post flight for examination of microflora.

Mice were implanted subcutaneously with radio frequency identification (RFID) chips (IMI-500, BMDS) at the vendor (Jackson Laboratory). Before launch, fecal pellets from each animal were collected at several different time points and each mouse was scanned via Dual-energy X-Ray Absorptiometry (DXA).

They received autoclaved, deionized water ad libitum, standard chow (LabDiet 5K52), then Nutrient Upgraded Rodent Food Bar (NuRFB). NuRFB foodbar changeout was every 14 days.

At launch plus (L+) 25 and L+26 days, 10 animals (consisting of 5 animals of each strain) were anesthetized and imaged with a bone density scanner, followed by exsanguination via cardiac puncture. Each animal was dissected for tissue collection (left lobe of liver, gastrointestinal tract, spleen) and the remaining carcass was sectioned into 3 parts (Head, Chest, and Abdomen/hindlimbs). All tissues and carcass sections were preserved in RNAlater and stored at -80C. Blood was collected, separated by
centrifugation, and then frozen and stored at -80C. The same procedures were L+75 and L+76 days for the remaining 10 animals. All samples from the first month of the mission, including carcasses of the first 10 mice, returned on SpX-15 and the remaining samples were returned on SpX-16.

Dissections were performed 2/2019 at Northwestern University.

RR-9.description:
The Rodent Research 9 (RR-9) payload consisted of three space biology experiments that examined the impacts of long-duration spaceflight on human tissue and systems, aiming to better understand the visual impairment and joint tissue degradation that affected astronauts and to investigate possible ways to counteract those health problems. One investigation studied the effects of microgravity on fluid shifts and increased fluid pressures that occurred in the head. A second examined the impact of spaceflight on the vessels that supplied blood to the eyes. The third investigated the extent of knee and hip joint degradation caused by prolonged exposure to weightlessness.

NASA's Space Life and Physical Sciences (SLPS) partnered with Russia's Institute of Biomedical Problems (IMBP) to establish a collaborative and multidisciplinary study to examine the effects of spaceflight on various physiological systems. This mission was sponsored by the NASA Space Biology Program.

The objectives of the Investigator team’s studies were to evaluate physiological changes in mice that occurred during a long-duration spaceflight mission in low Earth orbit. Maximal science return was achieved by distributing dissected tissues from the animals to as many Russian and NASA investigators as possible via the SLPS Biospecimen Sharing Program (BSP) and through agreements with the IMBP.

Twenty (20) mice (male, C57BL/6) between 8–16 weeks old were launched in one Transporter (10 mice per side), transferred to Rodent Habitats onboard the International Space Station (ISS), and maintained in microgravity for approximately 30 days (the SpaceX Dragon docked period). Nominally, no crew activities were required except for standard animal transfers between the Transporter and Habitats, and other activities required to ensure animal welfare, such as health checks and NuRFB replenishments.
Prior to Dragon unberth, all twenty mice were transferred into a clean Transporter, followed by transfer to a Dragon capsule and then returned to Earth alive (live animal return [LAR]). The duration from splashdown to handover of the mice payload was approximately 48–72 hours. After the handover of the mice to the NASA Rodent Research team, the mice were immediately transported to a facility approved for conducting post-flight rodent gait assessment and dissections. This facility was located as close to the payload handover location as possible to minimize the total duration the mice were exposed to 1G post-splashdown. The primary investigator teams, BSP teams, and the Rodent Research dissection Lead and team conducted the dissection process at this facility immediately following a health check, specimen sampling, and acquisition of walking kinematic data.

The Rodent Research 9 (RR-9) science investigation was conducted by the National Aeronautics and Space Administration’s Space Life and Physical Sciences program. The mission consisted of three experiments led by principal investigators Michael Delp, Xiao Wen Mao, and Jeffrey Willey. Delp’s investigation studied the effects of long-duration spaceflight on fluid shifts and increased fluid pressures in the head, Mao’s examined the impact of spaceflight on the vessels that supplied blood to the eyes, and Willey’s investigated the extent of knee and hip joint degradation caused by prolonged exposure to weightlessness. Specific aims of each experiment are summarized below.

The mission objectives

Michael Delp’s experiment had four aims:
-	To determine whether spaceflight on the ISS altered rodent basilar artery spontaneous tone, myogenic and KCl (Potassium Chloride)-evoked vasoconstriction, mechanical stiffness, and gross structure.
-	To estimate whether spaceflight on the ISS altered the blood-brain barrier in rodents, as indicated by ultrastructural examination of the junctional complex of the cerebral capillary endothelium.
-	To determine whether spaceflight on the ISS altered rodent basal vein (inside cranium) and jugular vein (outside cranium) spontaneous tone, myogenic and KCl-evoked constriction, distension, and gross structure.
-	To determine whether spaceflight on the ISS altered the ability of the cervical lymphatics to modulate lymph flow, and thus, regulate cerebral fluid homeostasis.

Xiao Wen Mao’s investigation had two aims:
-	To define the relationships between spaceflight condition-induced oxidative stress in reactive oxygen species (ROS) expression and retinal vascular remodeling and BRB function in mice that returned to Earth alive.
-	To determine whether spaceflight condition-induced oxidative damage in the retina was mediated through photoreceptor mitochondrial ROS production.

Jeffrey Willey’s investigation had two aims:
-	To determine the extent of knee and hip joint degradation in mice after 30 days of spaceflight on the ISS.
-	To use the DigiGait System to assess gait patterns before and after returning from the ISS.

IACUC Protocol Number: FLT-17-107

All animal procedures performed in these experiments were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committees (IACUC), with protocol numbers NASA: FLT-17-107 for flight at the NASA Ames Research Center (ARC) and the Kennedy Space Center (KSC), and the methods were carried out in accordance with relevant guidelines and regulations.
